articles.title: Resident Evil : on tient le meilleur film de la saga et l'un des plus jouissifs de l'année
articles.text:
Concrètement, ce reboot de Resident Evil signé Zach Cregger arrive dans les salles françaises ce mercredi 16 septembre 2026. Austin Abrams y incarne Bryan, un livreur médical qui se retrouve pris au piège d’une nuit d’épouvante à Raccoon City.
Aller voir ce film Resident Evil dès son premier jour d’exploitation restait un pari risqué, mais la réaction du public ne trompe pas avec des applaudissements à la fin de la séance. La première force du film est d’avoir envoyé valser le fan-service bas du plafond. Exit les icônes intouchables comme Leon S. Kennedy ou Jill Valentine, dont le grand écran a déjà massacré la crédibilité à maintes reprises.
Le contexte aide à comprendre ce choix : le film déroule une histoire inédite, coécrite par Cregger et Shay Hatten, qui se cale sur les événements de Resident Evil 2 sans reprendre aucun personnage des jeux. Le réalisateur a même reconnu n’avoir jamais vu les six films précédents, portés par Milla Jovovich entre 2002 et 2017.
Cregger, réalisateur de talent derrière Évanouis, préfère planter le décor avec des inconnus et se concentrer sur la sève du jeu, la peur panique d’un type ordinaire coincé dans un couloir sombre.
Une fidélité viscérale aux mécaniques du jeu vidéo pour le film Resident Evil
Cette fidélité aux jeux Resident Evil passe par une véritable montée en puissance matérielle de l’angoisse. On suit ce livreur médical complètement dépassé, campé par un Austin Abrams parfait en antihéros sous anxiolytiques, qui commence son calvaire à poil, armé de son (absence de) courage, avant de dénicher des pétoires de plus en plus « puissantes » au fil de sa descente aux enfers.
L’humour découle naturellement de cette mécanique rétro, le film se moque ouvertement de l’architecture absurde de Raccoon City, où la moindre porte de réserve nécessite trois clés ornées et quatre cadenas thématiques. Quant aux monstres, on retrouve du traumatisant qui rappelle les meilleures heures du cinéma des années 80, notamment The Thing, dont l’inspiration est manifeste.
Le gore généreux terrasse les jump scares
Sur le terrain de l’épouvante pure, Cregger refuse de couper les angles pour plaire aux adolescents en quête de frissons tièdes. La violence y est brutale, graphique et sans aucune concession, réservant quelques démembrements particulièrement croustillants qui ont fait grincer des dents la moitié de la salle. Surtout, le réalisateur redonne des lettres de noblesse au jump scare. Loin des ficelles téléphonées du tout-venant hollywoodien, chaque hausse de tension est construite avec un sens de la rupture qui fait bondir de son siège même les spectateurs les plus blasés.
Tout n’est pas parfait pour autant dans ce carnage réjouissant. On regrettera amèrement que le film succombe par moments au syndrome du héros qui commente absolument tout ce qu’il fait à voix haute pour meubler le silence ou rassurer le public. Cette manie insupportable de verbaliser chaque décision, « D’accord, je dois atteindre ce couloir, attraper cette clé et ne pas me faire bouffer », s’inscrit pile dans cette tare récurrente du cinéma contemporain qui prend le spectateur pour un analphabète visuel.
C’est agaçant, mais fort heureusement, le vacarme des fusillades et le bruit des os qui craquent viennent rapidement étouffer ces accès d’explication de texte.
Un poil trop de numérique ?
Même si la mise en scène claque et que Cregger sait poser une ambiance, le film se prend parfois les pieds dans le tapis du blockbuster moderne. Le gore a beau couler à flots, il faut bien avouer que pas mal de giclées de sang et de tripes baveuses carburent aux effets numériques un peu grossiers, ce qui enlève parfois un peu de matière à l’angoisse. Rien de rédhibitoire pour ruiner la séance, mais on sent la patte du studio qui repasse par-dessus pour en rajouter des caisses en post-production là où la sobriété aurait suffi.
Une expérience de salle obligatoire pour enterrer le passé
Oubliez les séances en solo sur votre canapé avec le téléphone à la main : ce reboot a été pensé comme un rituel collectif, où la peur se partage à plusieurs dans le noir. articles.title: Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is incredibly ambitious but frustratingly bloated
articles.text:
“Ugh… The scale of all this… I’m starting to get a headache.”
Leda, one of the protagonists of Intelligent System’s Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave, makes this comment late into the strategy RPG’s campaign. She’s referring to the cataclysmic threat posed by the main villain, the demon king Balor, but incidentally, it’s also the perfect description of how I feel towards Fortune’s Weave as a whole.
While the game has a staggeringly intricate structure that weaves between three distinct arcs, the breadth and depth of all of its content proves to overbearing. The overall gameplay loop and some individual narrative beats certainly shine, but they’re unfortunately bogged down by copious amounts of excess. The end result is an entertaining, but wildly uneven, strategy-RPG experience.
A sprawling, but unfocused, epic
Right off the bat, Fortune’s Weave positions itself as a rather novel entry in the Fire Emblem series. That’s because it’s set in the same universe as 2019’s Three Houses but takes place hundreds of years later in a different land across the sea. Truthfully, it initially feels a bit like dangling keys in front of Three Houses fans, with the game opening with the Progenitor God Sothis (a returning Cassandra Lee Morris) once again teeing up your journey. But otherwise, this is entirely standalone from Three Houses.
That standalone nature is not inherently a bad thing, to be sure, although those inherent connections do make the story here feel comparatively trite. While Three Houses focused on the Game of Thrones-esque conflict between clans and a sympathetic villain who aimed to end this violent, prejudicial cycle, Fortune’s Weave is simply about the world-ending monster Balor. The game begins in this post-apocalyptic future he’s brought about, with protagonist Eshmel being sent back in time five years to change the fate of four “Flame Lords” who will aid in humanity’s last ditch effort to survive.
This is where Fortune’s Weave‘s ambition really comes to bear, as each Flame Lord, quite impressively, has their own full-sized campaign. Leda, the character I started with because of her unique musical abilities, is a minstrel who seeks vengeance for her father’s murder. Theodora, meanwhile, must take over her kingdom once her own father is killed, while Cai, a young boy, seeks to save his father from imprisonment. (Fortune’s Weave really likes paternal motivations, apparently.) And the fourth and final Flame Lord, Dietrich, is simply in it for the love of the game as he roams the land to find worthy opponents.
They all come to Dagda, a bustling Greco-Roman city, to take part in the Heroic Games, a coliseum-style tournament in which the winner is granted one wish by the church of state. And once you complete Part I of a given campaign, that Flame Lord and their allies and gear can be brought into two additional Parts, the middle of which directly segues into the final Balor section. It’s a riveting hook, especially if you play with Permadeath enabled as I did, as it feels genuinely rewarding to have successfully levelled up and guided these characters throughout the entire campaign. (And, similarly, this makes it all the more devastating should you lose any units along the way.)
There are several weaknesses within this years-spanning epic, however. For one, Balor is the most generic of apocalyptic threats, while Eshmel (who you can customize as male or female) is a practically voiceless avatar with no actual personality or dimension. As such, you simply have no attachment to either character, which causes the late stretch of the game, which took me 20-plus hours, to really suffer. Worse still, their conflict feels so jarringly disconnected from the Heroic Games. You go from a character-driven narrative with relatively low stakes (all while a larger Dagdan conspiracy is teased but never fully fleshed out) to a cataclysmic battle against a dime-a-dozen creature that really has nothing to do with the Flame Lords.
But even ignoring the Eshmel-Balor side of the game, the first two parts that lead into it are inconsistent at best. As Leda, I spent around 40 hours during the Tournament Arc, and this features a pretty rote story about the corrosive, maddening nature of revenge that also unfolds at a glacial pace due to its repetitious “match, break, match, break” structure, with plot developments being slowly drip-fed in between. Worse still, Leda’s campaign in Part II (the “War Arc”) suddenly makes her a supporting character to Theodora as the latter’s people engage in a deadly conflict with another kingdom. It’s a baffling decision to effectively reduce Leda’s role to a glorified cameo in her own story to shift focus for 10 or so hours to another protagonist in whom we have no investment.
This proves especially frustrating because the game’s insistence on making everything so elongated means that switching to going through Theodora’s campaign isn’t something you can quickly do. To be clear, I love the multiple campaigns of games like Nier Automata and Kingdom Hearts Birth by Sleep because they’re manageably sized, taking around 10 hours each and, thus, allowing me to see the bigger narrative picture in a reasonable amount of time. Fortune’s Weave, though, seems to want to punish you for not dedicating another 40 hours at least just to see other highly relevant perspectives. It feels like the Marvel Cinematic Universe at its worst, making you do “homework” with seemingly unrelated stories so you’re properly prepared for the one you actually came to see.
And of course, I can really only speak for Leda and the several hours I subsequently played of Theodora’s story, the latter of which did admittedly seem more interesting than simply “vengeance” due to its focus on the religious discrimination experienced by the nascent queen and her people. Given the staggeringly massive scope of Fortune’s Weave, I simply wasn’t able to check out Cai or Dietrich’s individual campaigns, with my only real engagement with them coming instead through incidental appearances they make during Leda’s Tournament Arc.
Perhaps the other three campaigns would have felt more cohesive (either in terms of connecting to Balor or even just standing on their own instead of this heavy MCU-like crossover), but to fully answer that question, I’d have had to play at least 200 hours before writing this review, which is simply ridiculous. Fortune’s Weave simply doesn’t respect your time.
Excellent strategy buried under lots of repetition
This sense of disjointedness extends well beyond narrative, although it takes a while for it to settle in, as Fortune’s Weave does indeed provide a legitimately engrossing gameplay loop at its core. In between tournament matches, you have an allotted number of in-game days to prepare in various ways, including by taking part in Dagdan activities like training or performances to raise stats and Bonds between allies.
The most meaningful element of Fortune’s Weave‘s calendar system, though, is the world map. Rather than being an open-world setting, you can move your character along this grid-like chart a few spaces at a time, with one turn passing along the way to inch you closer to the looming tournament match. At first, this might seem like a limitation, but I quickly came to appreciate just how much more conscientious I became about how I was spending my time.
To complete sidequests, including the character-specific ones (in Leda’s case, reaching various towns to perform music), I had to carefully plan my route for maximum efficiency, taking into account obstacles like enemies and shifting environments (i.e. a desert that slows your traversal) and making full use of carriages that offer limited fast travel opportunities. It adds to the strategic ethos at the heart of Fire Emblem in a thoughtful way.
The world map is also vast enough to encourage exploration, as venturing off the main paths may unlock hidden villages, little areas with rare loot or even dungeons. That last element is especially worth your while.
In a welcome return from the excellent 3DS game Fire Emblem Echoes: Shadows of Valentia, dungeons are 3D environments that you can fully run around in to find chests and resources. Enemies can also be struck to give you a leg up in battles, which are represented here through Clashes, Final Fantasy-esque turn-based battles with a row of party members instead of Fire Emblem‘s signature bird’s eye view, tile-based combat. All in all, dungeons offer a refreshing change of pace, although their relatively copy-and-paste visual design and layouts leave much to be desired. (Get ready to see lots of uninspired, run-of-the-mill caves.)
And because the world map exploration is so full of rewards, the classic turn-based battles feel that much more impactful. I put in all of that work to acquire that extra gear, level up that character or complete that particular sidequest, and so I would head into fights feeling gratifyingly prepared. This is especially important because Fortune’s Weave has an annoying tendency to constantly throw many (often respawning) enemies at you in story battles, even on Normal difficulty, which I inevitably switched back to from Hard in Part III, the “Salvation Arc,” due to how unrelenting it became.
I am happy to report, if nothing else, that the one major new combat gimmick that Fortune’s Weave introduces is rather brilliant. Enter Blaze Arts, which are special Flame Lord moves that cost HP in exchange for huge benefits. Leda, for instance, can strum her vihuela instrument to dramatically buff allies and even clear environmental hazards, while Theodora is able to hurl chunks of the earth for long-range attacks.
Use enough of these moves (or special high-level weapons), and you’ll enter Overblaze, a super-powered state that increases your strength, but use too many and you’ll Burst, reducing your maximum HP for the rest of the fight. It’s a brilliant risk-reward mechanic, challenging you to let it rip at the right moment lest you weaken your central units too early.
With all of that said, the nature of Fortune’s Weave, segmented as it is by four campaigns, means that there’s only a handful of actually developed characters throughout. This means that the vast majority of the units that you’ll recruit to fill out your party are painfully thin. As you run around Dagda, you’ll encounter people who will join your cause, provided you meet arbitrary criteria like sharing a minimum Bond level with them (raised by inviting them to local activities like going to meals or shows together) or high enough Renown (a gauge that increases by completing sidequests and other activities on the world map).
But despite those hefty requirements to unlock them, they don’t actually have any fleshed-out narrative of their own, practically no backstory and certainly no Support conversations to speak of. Not even Seteth, the saintly warrior who returns from Three Houses as a recruitable character, has any actual scenes with the Flame Lords, Eshmel or any of the other cast. It feels almost insulting to force you to grind so much to recruit that one character, and then they don’t have any unique story material besides a few canned lines, making them feel interchangeable and even disposable. People bemoaned the heavy social elements in Three Houses, but those, at least, always felt meaningful because all of the students and teachers had their own backstories and Support conversations to make them feel like living, breathing people as well as combat units.
The limited characterization in Fortune’s Weave proves especially glaring should you complete special Paralogue sidequests for some of the Flame Lords or their close allies in other campaigns. Doing so actually allows you to let them join you in the Salvation Arc even if you didn’t complete their campaigns, which feels like the rare time Fortune’s Weave actually forgives you for not doing everything. But even then, it leads to these hilarious MCU-esque guest roles in which characters like Dietrich became suddenly allied with me in the late-game even though I had zero context for who they were.
This also raises another critical issue: playing with Permadeath but not engaging with at least two campaigns severely kneecaps you. By the time I reached Part III, I had lost numerous allies (fatalities brought about, in no small part, due to playing on Hard for most of the game), and in this final stretch, the opportunities to recruit new units are limited outside of a few who join per the narrative or Paralogue completion. Your only other recourse, as the game keeps telling you, is to go back in time and guide the other Flame Lords to the future. In other words, Fortune’s Weave is, once again, punishing you for not putting at least 100 hours into the game.
All the while, the Salvation Arc feels dragged out due to its own structure. Essentially, you’re free to challenge Balor whenever, although naturally, you’ll need to be sufficiently levelled. What’s more, the Demon King summons Underworld Gates that you have to destroy within an allotted calendar period. None of this is inherently problematic, but as with so much of the game, it’s unnecessarily bloated. That’s because the Gates are often spread across the map, forcing you to split your units into smaller parties to divide and conquer, all while keeping one unit near Dagda to protect advancing waves of enemies.
The first or second time I had to do this, it proved quite captivating, challenging me to strategically deploy parties that were as balanced as possible while also saving a few to keep an eye on Dagda. It was a clever evolution of the earlier world map exploration that kept me on my toes. But having to do this several more times, with the gaps between the placement of the gates widening throughout and the individual map points that you have to reach to dispel barriers protecting them, just felt unbearably tedious.
Compounding this frustration is the fact the maps for Act 3’s story battles are all filled with their own unique forms of miasma, which coat many tiles with significant stat-reducing penalties that rarely even affect enemies. It’s yet another example of Fortune’s Weave being big for the sake of it, and it proved grating in those final hours.
Fortune favours the slog
Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave can be an exasperating game. For all of the meaningful ways it builds on the series’ central gameplay loop, particularly through an ingenious multi-act, cross-campaign approach to cause and effect and its densely layered world map, its insistence on maximalist game design regrettably harms the pacing, flow and RPG elements of the whole experience. Ultimately, I enjoyed the totality of the experience, but it really wore me out at times, and it leaves me begging Intelligent Systems to go with a “less is more” approach in future Fire Emblem games.
Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave launches exclusively on Nintendo Switch 2 on September 17.

articles.title: iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max review: better in all the right places
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max take last year’s Pro reinvention and refine it in all the right places — but the cameras are where Apple has made the biggest leap, with a variable aperture and finally useful Pro controls giving you more creative freedom without sacrificing the effortless shooting iPhone is known for. The A20 Pro brings plenty of power, battery life is excellent, thermals are noticeably better, and Siri AI finally starts delivering on Apple’s long-running promise. Neither phone is a night-and-day upgrade from the 17 Pro generation, but taken together, these improvements, as well as longer battery life and a smaller Dynamic Island, make the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max incredibly capable flagships that feel built to last.
Pros
- +Excellent camera system with genuinely useful Pro controls
- +Variable aperture adds creative flexibility
- +Burgundy and Glacier colors are beautiful
- +A20 Pro is very, very fast and enables long battery life
Cons
- -No major design changes
- -$100 / £100 / AU$100 more
Why you can trust TechRadar
Apple iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max: Two-Minute Review
If the iPhone 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max were a reinvention of the flagship iPhone, the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max see Apple carrying the flagship-iPhone baton forward with few, if any, missteps.
I’ve spent the last week with a Glacier iPhone 18 Pro Max and a Burgundy iPhone 18 Pro — both colors are striking new additions to Apple’s iPhone color palette — and Apple has mostly stuck to last year's winning formula, while updating key aspects of the experience to push things forward.
While the main camera array still carries the same 48-megapixel count across the telephoto, ultra-wide, and main lenses, the arrival of Pro controls in the Camera app breathes new life into the photo-taking experience, letting you get seriously creative whenever you want to.
You can also take advantage of the new variable aperture on the main 48-megapixel Fusion camera to shoot across ƒ/1.48, ƒ/1.8, ƒ/2.8, or ƒ/4.0, and capture unique visuals, including starburst effects from lights. Of course, you can also choose to let the Camera app take control, and in general it’ll capture a well-balanced shot that you can still edit after the fact.
All in all, after taking hundreds of photos and shooting dozens of videos, I’m impressed with the level of detail the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max can deliver. Some images match what you’ll get from the previous-generation Pros, but these iPhones can also deliver even better-looking images and video, especially when you take control.
Under the hood is Apple’s first 2-nanometer chip in an iPhone, the A20 Pro, and while it doesn’t run laps around the previous A19 Pro, or the chip before that one, its CPU, GPU, and Neural Engine do an excellent job of handling general iOS tasks, as well as more advanced AI features, including keeping Siri AI chugging along where it's available and powering Apple Intelligence features in Photos, such as Clean Up and Reframing. It also ensures that third-party experiences run well, and I’ll be shocked if you encounter noticeable slowdowns anywhere.
The iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max can easily keep pace with any of the other best modern smartphones, and I suspect they’ll keep doing so for years. You can again choose between a punchy, vibrant, and crisp 6.3-inch or 6.9-inch Super Retina XDR display, and that’s the main difference between the two Pro iPhones, as Apple maintains feature parity across the lineup.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Another meaningful improvement is in battery life, with the iPhone 18 Pro lasting longer than the 17 Pro Max according to Apple, while it says the 18 Pro Max establishes a new iPhone battery-life record. Add in the improved thermal management, smaller Dynamic Island, and arrival of Siri AI, and there’s a lot of refinement here beyond the cameras and processor.
And that’s ultimately what the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max feel like to me: a refinement of an already excellent Pro iPhone, rather than a reinvention. If the iPhone 17 Pro generation was about Apple changing the formula, the iPhone 18 Pro is about taking that formula and making it better across the board, without messing with what worked.
It’s not night and day across the board, and if you’re coming from an iPhone 17 Pro or 17 Pro Max, you probably don’t need to upgrade. The A20 Pro feels largely neck and neck with the A19 Pro in daily use, the displays remain familiar, and the overall design is essentially unchanged. But I would bet that some iPhone 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max owners will want to make the jump anyway, particularly for the camera improvements. The combination of the variable aperture and, finally, a genuinely customizable Camera app with Pro controls enables a level of user input that I’ve wanted Apple to bake into the iPhone for years.
If you’re holding onto an iPhone 15 Pro, 15 Pro Max, or anything older, the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max represent a much more substantial generational leap. You’re getting bigger and better displays, way-improved cameras, better battery life, a faster and more future-ready chip, improved thermals, and a modern, durable design that Apple has now had a year to refine.
And that’s the thing about the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max: you don’t need any one of these upgrades to completely reinvent how you use an iPhone. Taken together, though, they make for a seriously capable flagship that feels ready for the next several years.
Apple iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max review: Price and Availability
- Starts at $1,199 / £1,199 / AU$2,099 for 256GB
- Both Pro models now offer 512GB, 1TB, and 2TB options
- On sale September 18, with preorders open now
Apple made the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max official at its September 9, 2026, ‘Surprise and Shine’ special event; preorders are open now, with an on-sale date of September 18.
The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199 in the US, £1,199 in the UK, and AU$2,099 in Australia, and the iPhone 18 Pro Max at $1,299 / £1,299 / AU$2,299, respectively. That means they come with a $100 / £100 / AU$100 increase in starting price over the iPhone 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max, while, like last year’s Pros, starting at 256GB of storage. Both can be configured with 512GB, 1TB, and 2TB of storage, with the latter now an option on both Pro models. You can choose from Burgundy, Glacier, Silver, and Black.
Both phones officially go on sale on September 18, 2026.
- Value score: 4 / 5
Apple iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max review: Design
- The 18 Pro keeps the 17 Pro’s aluminum body and camera plateau
- Burgundy and Glacier colors bring some welcome personality to the Pro lineup
- A new vapor chamber and Nanotwin copper help keep things cooler under load
With the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max, Apple chose to dramatically reinvent the Pro-series iPhone's design. It swapped the left-side bump that housed the main camera system for a plateau that stretches across the back, went back to aluminum, and focused heavily on durability.
Given that, the odds of a major redesign for the next-gen Pro phones were slim, and the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max stick with a design that not only scored well in our reviews, but also won over a wider audience. I've been switching between the iPhone 17 Pro Max in Cosmic Orange and the iPhone Air for the last year.
The iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max stick with the aluminum body and camera plateau from last year's models. That might seem like a safe choice, considering that the iPhone Duo is launching alongside these candy-bar-style phones in October, but it also shows Apple pushing forward with a working design — essentially the same trajectory it took from the iPhone 16 to the iPhone 17.
Still, to help the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max stand out from the crowd — and just to let people know you’re rocking one of Apple’s new phones, rather than a 17 Pro or 17 Pro Max — there are two entirely new colors, and I can't decide which is my favorite, and luckily I've been testing both. Burgundy is sort of a dark-red wine color that evokes a sense of high-class sleekness, while Glacier, which the event invite teased, is a mix of blue and silver that looks decidedly fresh. These are the two colors that pop, both much more muted than Cosmic Orange, but also a bit more vibrant than the Dark Navy from 2025. Those two join silver and the first ‘true’ black Pro model. It shows that Apple is listening, and I'm all for more Pro colors.
The dimensions are the same year over year. The iPhone 18 Pro measures 150 x 71.9 x 8.75mm, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max comes in at 163.4 x 78 x 8.75mm — exactly the same footprint as their predecessors. The button placement is also identical, so if you've spent the last year with an iPhone 17 Pro or 17 Pro Max, there's nothing new to learn here: power and Camera Control are on the right, with the Action Button, and volume up and volume down on the left. Both phones are a little heavier than last year’s: the 18 Pro weighs 211 grams, up from 206 grams, while the 18 Pro Max jumps to 249 grams from 233 grams.
Even with the slight weight increase, both the 6.3-inch Pro and 6.9-inch Pro Max feel comfortable in the hand and are pretty well balanced. The Pro Max is still very much a two-handed phone for me, especially for texting, while the Pro is still the smaller, more portable option.
Then there's Ceramic Shield 2, which is sticking around. Judging by the coatings on my iPhone Air and 17 Pro Max, it's done wonders at preventing micro-abrasions and front-screen scratches, and even means that drops don’t elicit a gasp, since after a year my screens are still unblemished. In my few days testing the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, I haven't seen a scratch on the front or abrasions on the back, which is both aluminum and glass.
The iPhone 17 Pro Max was known for getting warm, or at least warmer to the touch, during more intense activities such as gaming or long content shoots, and Apple has looked to address that issue with some new cooling tech under the hood. There's a new thermal architecture inside, which consists of a vapor chamber, the positioning of which has been tweaked, and which offers three times the surface area to better dissipate heat. Apple has paired this with an industry-first Nanotwin copper material, which is baked into the display plate to help keep that surface cool.
For the most part, this has kept the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max cool during my testing. They can still get warm, but nowhere near as warm as the 17 Pro or 17 Pro Max, and the heat is more spread out when it does become noticeable. I noticed it mostly heating up during longer capture sessions, especially when swapping between photo and video, but even then the heat felt more spread out and better regulated, and dissipated more quickly.
It's a subtle change, but one that matters when you're using the phone heavily. And that's really the story of the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max design: Apple hasn't reinvented the wheel this year. Instead, it's taken the design it introduced with the iPhone 17 Pro and refined the parts that matter — durability, thermals, finishes, and how the phone feels during sustained use.
- Design score: 5 / 5
Apple iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max review: Display
- Two sizes, same experience across both
- A new anti-reflective coating joins 3,000 nits peak brightness and120Hz ProMotion
- Smaller Dynamic Island with room for three Live Activities
Your main decision when choosing between the 18 Pro and the 18 Pro Max comes down to size, as there’s feature parity between the two, and that’s a good thing. The iPhone 18 Pro features a 6.3-inch display, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max has a 6.9-inch display. Both are punchy, vibrant, and a joy to look at and use for any task, be it FaceTiming with friends or loved ones, typing out comms, reading an email, browsing the web, scrolling your photos, watching video, or just navigating iOS elements.
Much of that comes from the fact that these are Super Retina XDR displays, which are OLED and always-on, meaning that even when the phone is locked, the screen dims down to still show you the time, widgets, and even notifications. Like the iPhone 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max before them, the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max have a buttery-smooth 120Hz ProMotion refresh rate and top out at a maximum brightness of 3,000 nits. It’s unlikely the phone will always run at that brightness, but suffice to say that even on a bright, humid, sunny day — and I mean it was really beating down — in Orlando, Florida, enjoying the sights, sounds, and rides of Disney World, I had no issues viewing content on the screen.
There’s also a new anti-reflective coating on the display, and while this isn’t a full Nano-texture coating like you’ll find on some of Apple’s other displays and the folding iPhone Duo, it’s a noticeable step up when it comes to reducing reflections and smudges. It’s particularly useful outdoors, where fewer reflections mean less fighting with the screen to see what’s actually on it. Compared to older iPhones, like the iPhone 16 and earlier models, this feels like a much bigger display upgrade.
There is one thing that really did catch my eye, though, and it’s the key change with the display: Apple has shrunk the Dynamic Island down on the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. It’s about the size of an extra-strength Tylenol liquid gel, and much less of a distraction at the top, if you could even call it that. In addition to the reduced size, the other big change is to Live Activities — the Dynamic Island can now support three, rather than two. So maybe it’s directions, music playback, and a timer, or if you’re on a flight, maybe it’s United Airlines showing the seat number, Flighty counting down your arrival time, and music playing in Music or Spotify.
I’m not saying you need to rush out to upgrade just for this if you have a 17 Pro or 17 Pro Max — although that might be the case for the cameras or battery life — but if you’re a fan of using this space, it’s definitely a super-functional quality-of-life upgrade.
- Display score: 5 / 5
Apple iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max review: Cameras
- Pro controls finally arrive to let you adjust aperture, shutter speed, white balance, and more.
- The 48MP Fusion main camera aperture is adjustable from ƒ/1.48 to ƒ/4.0
- Better detail, strong low-light performance, and excellent 4x and 8x zoom
Alright, buckle in, because while the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max still boasts 48-megapixel main, 48-megapixel ultra-wide, and a 48-megapixel telephoto camera — similar to the iPhone 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max setup — things are a bit different across the board, and especially in one specific area.
For starters, if you’ve been wanting Apple to bake more controls into the Camera app, your wish has been granted. There are now Pro controls that let you adjust the aperture, shutter speed, and white balance for the main camera, alongside a host of other tools, including improved Photographic Styles, with more granular controls, and the ability to bring up a histogram.
You can also customize which of these controls live at the top of your screen, in a similar fashion to designing your perfect home screen or Control Center. Changes to shutter speed and aperture are persistent if you have that enabled in Settings for preserving camera settings, but you can’t design exact presets with a specific aperture or shutter speed, although — hint, Apple — that would be a nice upgrade.
Photographic Styles are also getting more flexible. You can still pick from the expected presets, but Apple now gives you more granular control over things like texture, including adjustments specifically aimed at skin. Push it in the right direction, and you can get smoother, more glowy-looking portraits, though there are times when that comes at the expense of some detail, particularly in lower-light areas of the frame.
That’s where I think Apple’s approach makes sense: the default Auto processing generally aims to strike a balance between detail, exposure, color, and skin tones, so you don’t have to think about any of this. But if you want to get more creative, the tools are there — and you can still make adjustments after the fact, rather than having to nail everything before you hit the shutter button.
Here’s a look at the camera specs, right before the big change that has to do with the main lens:
- 48MP Fusion main with variable aperture of ƒ/1.48, ƒ/1.8, ƒ/2.8, or ƒ/4.0
- 48MP Fusion ultra-wide at ƒ/2.2
- 48MP Fusion telephoto at ƒ/2.8
With these, you can still shoot at 0.5x, 1x at 24mm, 28mm, or 35mm, 2x for a digital crop with optical-quality results, 4x (as a digital sensor crop), or an optical 8x, and stretch all the way up to 40x digital zoom.
The big change, though, is that the main lens — the one your iPhone is set to by default — has a variable aperture for the first time ever on an iPhone. With a fine eye, or another camera pointed at it, you can actually see the lens aperture adjusting, getting wider or narrower to let more or less light in. It also swaps the previous main aperture of ƒ/1.78 on 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max, as the 18 Pro’ now offering ƒ/1.48, ƒ/1.8, ƒ/2.8, and ƒ/4.0.
You can choose to ignore this new control, as well as the ability to adjust white balance or shutter speed, and let the iPhone and its image-processing pipeline automatically engage what it believes are the optimum settings to capture a great shot. And in my testing so far, it succeeds here, offering on-par quality with the iPhone 17 Pro or 17 Pro Max, but mostly punching above those phones with better details, more natural blurring and focus points, and excellent highlights.
The image-processing pipeline has also been updated. Performance still feels very much in line with what I’ve come to expect from an iPhone, but images are more detailed and sharper throughout, though at times they can pack a little more punch with colors thanks to some update on the image pipeline. Especially for 4x and 8x shots, I’ve found that these preserve more details generation over generation. It’s not a dramatic departure from the iPhone look, but there’s a clear refinement here in how the phone handles detail and brings a scene to life.
The 4x and 8x zoom continued to surprise me with how much detail they can deliver, namely with the former being a sensor crop and the latter being optical. Whether I’m picking out details around Disney World’s parks or zooming in on something far away, the results stay impressively detailed without looking like a processed digital crop.
The variable aperture gives the main camera more flexibility, especially when you want to control how much light comes in, or how much of a subject is separated from the background. The wider maximum aperture also helps make this excellent main camera even more versatile in lower-light scenarios, and because it’s the camera your iPhone defaults to, it’s likely the one you’ll navigate to first.
The Most Magical Place on Earth deserves the best camera on a phone on Earth, right? So I’ve done the bulk of my iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max camera testing around the Disney World parks in Orlando, and taken plenty of additional shots in New Jersey, California, and even up in the sky from the windows of planes. That means I’ve tested the cameras in just about every condition I could throw at them, from the beating Florida sun to nighttime attractions, indoor spaces, moving subjects, and everything in between.

I’ve been putting the low-light performance to the test around Disney World, too, including taking plenty of shots after the sun went down. Even in Auto mode, I found the iPhone 18 Pro could deliver detail-packed, appropriately lit shots in less time, with Night mode often requiring less time to capture a shot than on previous generations. This comes down to about one to three seconds, versus five to eight seconds for processing. And that means less waiting around for the camera to finish its exposure and, more importantly, less chance of a moving subject turning into a blurry mess. You can accomplish longer exposures if the iPhone detects it’s in a tripod as well.
When I wanted more control, though, I could jump in and adjust the shutter speed and aperture when shooting at 1x or 2x zoom, letting me decide how I wanted to capture the scene, rather than leaving it entirely up to the iPhone. If you’re willing to take the time to dive into the controls, you can really customize how the iPhone captures a scene, and get much more creative with your shots.
For instance, I shot the Magic of Disney Animation building at night at ƒ/1.48 and 1/30s, deliberately opening up the aperture and slowing the shutter to let in more light. The result is a detail-packed shot with rich colors and a dramatic nighttime look, as you can see above. It’s still an iPhone, so you can absolutely leave everything on Auto and get a great photo, but when you want to take more control, the tools are there to help you capture the shot you have in your mind’s eye.
The same Pro controls carry over to video, giving you more control over how you capture moving footage. There’s also a new auto-tracking feature, and I’ve found it particularly useful for fast-moving subjects.
I put it to the test at Disney World with Slinky Dog Dash, capturing the coaster as it came down the sloping track. The iPhone did a great job of keeping the front of the coaster in focus while the people blurred with the speed of the ride, and the lighting on the track moving alongside the vehicles stayed remarkably clear. The shot came out incredibly well, and it really shows what the iPhone can do with a fast-moving subject.
The 18-megapixel front-facing camera is essentially unchanged from last year, but that’s not necessarily a bad thing, as the Center Stage camera still uses that clever square sensor, letting you rotate between portrait and landscape framing without physically turning the iPhone. Better yet, it will still automatically adjust to fit more people in the shot.
The cameras are easily the most exciting part of the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, and as in years and generations past, it’s a big reason why folks go Pro. You get three capable shooters, and the ability to step back or step closer, depending on what you’re trying to capture. This year, Apple is giving you more control, and adding a genuinely neat upgrade to the main camera. The choice is ultimately yours: you can stick with Auto and still capture great shots, or make your mark with adjustments and shoot more intentionally.
Yes, third-party apps have offered many of these controls before, but having them baked right into the native Camera app can make a big impact, in my opinion. You don’t have to download another app or learn another interface to take advantage of them — they’re right there when you open the camera.
- Camera score: 5 / 5

Apple iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max review: Software, Siri AI, and Apple Intelligence
- Siri AI is here, in beta, and works across apps and personal context
- It can use your current on-screen context to help answer questions
- It's a major step forward, but it still makes mistakes and has rough edges
The iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max ran iOS 26 out of the box, and it's no surprise that iOS 27 is preloaded on the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. It runs really well here, and the A20 Pro under the hood keeps things gliding along — more on that processor below.
Much of iOS 27 is about under-the-hood changes that speed things up, which is especially helpful for older phones, along with more ways to customize the Liquid Glass interface, including adjusting how much of that glass effect you want to see.
The real story, though, is that the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max come with the new, AI-powered Siri out of the box, in beta, in specific regions. It’s available now in the United States, though you’ll need to join a waitlist, and it arrives alongside some new Apple Intelligence features.
For starters, Siri AI is much faster, and shows its work as it goes, which makes the experience feel more transparent. For instance, I’ve asked for details on my last flight and watched Siri AI dive into the right app — whether that’s Calendar, Flighty, United, or even Mail — to pull up the information I’m looking for. I’ve also used it to confirm my departure time, and ask how long it might take to get to the airport. It really does work, and it feels natural, and easy to get the hang of.
That doesn’t mean it’s perfect. Siri AI diving into some apps can cause mistakes, and at times it can pull up the wrong dataset or make the wrong assumption about what I’m asking for. But given how delayed this upgrade has been, and how limited the existing Siri has felt, overall it finally feels like Apple has delivered on the promise of a more capable assistant, while still putting privacy at the center as it works with your personal data and what’s on your device.
Siri AI can even be cued to see what’s on your screen, adding another layer of usefulness. Rather than having to explain everything you’re looking at, you can let Siri understand the context of what’s in front of you and go from there. It’s one of those features that sounds small on paper, but once you start using it, it feels like the direction Siri should have been heading in all along.
Apple Intelligence also brings a handful of other updates, including new ways to work with images, improvements to Photos and other apps, and more ways to put on-device intelligence to work. But Siri AI is easily the headline for me. After years of Siri feeling like an assistant that was increasingly behind the times, it finally feels like I’m actually talking to an AI assistant on an iPhone, rather than simply giving commands to a voice interface.
And while it’s still in beta, and there are clearly some kinks to work out, that’s an important distinction. Apple isn’t just talking about what Siri will be able to do anymore — on the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, I’m actually using it. It’s faster, more conversational, understands more context, and can work across the apps and information already on my phone.
For me, that makes iOS 27 feel less like a flashy annual software update, and more like the foundation for where Apple wants the iPhone to go next. The A20 Pro gives it the horsepower to keep everything moving, while Siri AI finally starts making good on the Apple Intelligence promise. And because it’s built into the iPhone, and designed around the information already on your device, it feels like a much more natural extension of how I already use my phone, rather than another AI chatbot I need to remember to open.
- Software score: 5 / 5
Apple iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max review: Performance
- A20 Pro is seriously fast
- The biggest gains over the A19 Pro come in specific workloads and future headroom
- Improved thermal management helps keep the phone cooler under heavy use
It might be no surprise, but the A20 Pro chip inside the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max is, as Apple claims, the fastest chip it’s put in an iPhone. And it’s actually more similar to an M-Series-powered SoC that Apple might opt for in a Mac than previous A-series chips.
With the A20 Pro, the SoC actually sits next to the DRAM, rather than having the memory stacked on top, as it has been in previous generations. It’s also built on a 2-nanometer process, just like the M6.
Inside the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, the A20 Pro is broken up into a 6-core CPU — two performance cores and four efficiency cores — a 7-core GPU, and a dual 16-core Neural Engine.
What does all of that mean for real-world use? Well, pretty much what you’d expect from a new Pro iPhone: everything is fast. Apps open quickly, jumping between them is fluid, games run smoothly, and even more demanding tasks don’t really give the A20 Pro much pause.
Take video exports, for example. I’ve been exporting 4K videos with graphics, text, and transitions in both Edits and CapCut, and the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max handle them quickly. It’s the kind of task where you can really feel the combination of the new chip and all that processing power, especially when you’re working with more complicated edits.
Gaming is another area where the A20 Pro flexes a bit. Real Flight Simulator runs smoothly, with environments rendering quickly as I’m flying around. The same goes for Wuthering Waves and Genshin Impact, both of which seemingly put a pretty serious load on the phones, which they seemingly handle without issue.
Multitasking has also been a non-issue. I’ve had plenty of apps open, jumped into FaceTime while playing a game, and bounced between multiple text conversations without the iPhone 18 Pro or 18 Pro Max missing a beat. That’s probably the less exciting side of performance, but it’s also where you notice the power of the A20 Pro day-to-day — you don’t really have to think about what’s running in the background.
Photo Clean Up is a bit faster than it was on the iPhone 17 Pro, for example, so removing an unwanted object or person from a shot takes less time. It’s not a massive difference, but when you use these tools frequently, those little speed improvements add up.
Additionally, the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max handle heat better, so sustained performance doesn’t come with the same uncomfortable warmth I experienced with the 17 Pro generation. The heat isn’t magically gone, but it’s distributed better, rather than sitting in one spot on the back, and dissipates faster.
It’s worth keeping some perspective here, though. The A20 Pro isn’t night-and-day faster than the A19 Pro in the iPhone 17 Pro or the chip in the iPhone Air, and you’ll likely only see more meaningful gains over something like the iPhone 16 Pro in specific scenarios. That’s not really the point.
The A20 Pro gives the iPhone more headroom for the future, especially as we run more and more AI-powered tasks on our phones, and, increasingly, other Apple devices. After spending this much time with it, the A20 Pro gives me no pause about getting several years of strong performance out of the iPhone 18 Pro or 18 Pro Max.
If you’re coming from an iPhone 15 or older, though, that’s where I think you’ll really notice the difference. You’re not just getting a faster chip; you’re getting a phone with considerably more processing headroom for demanding games, video editing, Apple Intelligence, and whatever Apple adds over the next few years.
Additionally, the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max will both feature the new Apple-made C2 modem globally. On my Burgundy iPhone 18 Pro connected to AT&T's network, I scored over 900MBps down in a jam-packed park, but the story is a little different with the 18 Pro Max in the US. The larger Pro iPhone in the States opts for a Qualcomm modem, but I didn't notice much of an issue with performance. I was connected to the Visible network and averaged about 350MBps to 500MBps down while in the parks and around New Jersey.
- Performance score: 5 / 5
Apple iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max review: Battery
- I averaged around 30 hours, with the Pro Max stretching further
- 50% charge in 15 minutes means you can get back in action quickly with wired charging
Alongside variable aperture on the main camera and the faster A20 Pro inside, Apple is making big promises about battery life with its latest Pro iPhones. In fact, the Cupertino giant notes that the iPhone 18 Pro will last longer than the iPhone 17 Pro Max, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max offers the longest battery life ever in an iPhone.
More specifically, it’s up to 36 hours of video playback on the iPhone 18 Pro, and up to 45 hours on the iPhone 18 Pro Max. These figures are based on Apple’s video-playback testing, and real-world battery life will vary depending on what you’re doing. Also keep in mind that these devices will need some time to index and get their bearings.
I’ll likely need to come back to this section in the coming weeks as indexing concludes, and I’m not shooting hundreds of photos and many minutes of video a day — after all, this is a review period. But with both the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, I’ve averaged around 30 hours of use before needing to plug in, and that stretches a bit further with the Max.
Even on an endurance day in the Florida heat, with hundreds of photos captured and nearly an hour of video recorded, the iPhone 18 Pro Max lasted an impressive amount of time before I needed a pit stop back at the hotel to recharge. It can drain quickly with heavy use, especially when you’re doing a lot of content capture, but in my testing thus far, both phones have been impressive.
In Future Labs' battery test, the iPhone 18 Pro lasted 16 hours and 17 minutes, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max ran for 18 hours and 27 minutes. That’s a good chunk less than Apple’s own video-playback figures, but my daily usage does stretch a bit closer to its claims.
On my last day of testing, I took the iPhone 18 Pro Max off the charger at 6AM and it hit 80% right before 11AM. With lots of app usage and some capture, it dropped to around 40% around 6PM with heavier use, but on average I got about 30 hours of use.
Apple also has improved fast wired charging, letting you hit 50% in just 15 minutes. I achieved that with both phones using Apple’s own Dynamic 40W charger, as well as a smaller Anker 45W Nano Cube. That means even if you do drain the battery, you don’t have to spend long tethered to an outlet before you’re back in business.
- Battery score: 5 / 5
Apple iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max: Should you buy?
| iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max scorecard |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Attributes | Notes | Rating | 
|---|---|---|
| Value | Even with the $100 / £100 / AU$100 price increase, both Pro models deliver enough meaningful upgrades to justify the premium. | 4 / 5 | 
| Design | A similar design that's now refined with better thermals and two fantastic new colors. | 5 / 5 | 
| Display | The Super Retina XDR OLEDs are still punchy, sharp, and smooth with ProMotion and Always-On functionality, and with a smaller Dynamic Island. | 5 / 5 | 
| Software | Siri AI finally feels like the smarter, more capable assistant Apple promised, and iOS 27 is plenty smooth. | 5 / 5 | 
| Camera | Apple finally gives you serious camera controls on the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, plus a genuinely useful variable aperture for the main lens. | 5 / 5 | 
| Performance | The A20 Pro is incredibly fast, efficient, and ready for whatever comes next. | 5 / 5 | 
| Battery | Outstanding endurance, with the Pro Max delivering the longest battery life on an iPhone. | 5 / 5 | 
Buy it if...
You want the best cameras
The iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max take their three 48MP cameras to the next level, adding a variable aperture to the main camera and Pro controls across the board.
Don’t buy it if...
You have an iPhone 17 Pro
The iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max refine last year’s formula rather than reinvent it, so the upgrade is less substantial, especially if you're not interested in the changes.
Apple iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max: Also consider
Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra
If you're alright with Android and want an excellent mix of performance and hardware, plus far-reaching zoom that can rival the iPhone, Samsung's latest and greatest candybar smartphone is worth a look.
Read our full Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra review
Apple iPhone Duo
It won't arrive until October, but if you're after a design revolution from Apple, the iPhone Duo will likely fit the bill as Cupertino's first foldable phone. It offers the same excellent performance as the 18 Pro, plus an extra screen.
Read our hands-on preview of the iPhone Duo
Apple iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max: How I tested
I’ve covered iPhones since the iPhone 8 generation, and the iPhone 3GS was my first personal iPhone. For this review, I spent a week with the iPhone 18 Pro in Burgundy and the iPhone 18 Pro Max in Glacier.
☑️ 100s of smartphones reviewed
☑️ 15 years of product testing
☑️ Over 16,000 products reviewed in total
☑️ Nearly 200,000 hours testing tech
I used both as daily drivers, covering everything from calls and streaming to gaming, work apps, photography, and video. I also ran performance benchmarks, tested multitasking and demanding workloads, and tracked battery drain across different usage scenarios alongside a standardized battery test.
For the cameras, I captured hundreds of photos and dozens of videos across Disney World — including Magic Kingdom, EPCOT, Hollywood Studios, and the resorts — as well as New Jersey, California, and from airplane windows. I tested every rear camera, multiple focal lengths, variable aperture, Pro controls, Night mode, Portrait mode, and video, along with the 18MP Center Stage camera.
I also compared the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max with the previous-generation Pro models, the iPhone 17, iPhone Air, and other smartphones including the Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro.
First reviewed September 2026.
Jacob Krol is the US Managing Editor, News for TechRadar. He’s been writing about technology since he was 14 when he started his own tech blog. He specializes in covering companies like Apple, Samsung, and Google and going hands-on with mobile devices, smart home gadgets, TVs, and wearables. articles.text:
Pick up a giant 18-inch RTX 5080-powered Asus gaming laptop from Best Buy and save $600 — the ROG Strix G18 also comes with 32GB of memory and a 2TB SSD
Game on a 2.5K resolution screen powered by an RTX 5080 laptop graphics card
Laptops have long been a more expensive way to game, especially compared to a desktop gaming PC, for comparable components. But with the ever-rising costs of PC hardware in the current economic climate, it's a lot easier and now often cheaper to get a powerful prebuilt gaming PC or ready-made gaming laptop. Today's deal is on a large, 18-inch Asus ROG Strix G18 gaming laptop powered by an RTX 5080, now reduced by $600 to $2,699.99. It's still an expensive piece of kit, but you are getting a somewhat portable form factor and a good amount of memory and storage included in the specs for this large gaming laptop.
● Check out this deal at Best Buy
Asus's ROG Strix G18 is a large 18-inch laptop with a big screen. The 18-inch display sports an IPS panel with a 240Hz refresh rate and 500-nit brightness. Powering the display and your gaming performance is an NVIDIA RTX 5080 laptop GPU that includes 16GB of fast GDDR7 VRAM, along with the 24-core Core Ultra 9 275HX processor from Intel. Importantly, there's also a good amount of memory: 32GB of DDR5 RAM and a large 2TB PCIe Gen4 SSD for storage.
A mighty 18-inch gaming laptop that uses a very powerful Nvidia RTX 5080 laptop GPU with 16GB of VRAM. The onboard processor is a 24-core Intel Core Ultra 9 275HX, sporting boost clock frequencies of up to 5.1 GHz, with an ample 32GB of DDR5 memory. There's also plenty of room for your game collection on the included 2TB SSD.
For any future upgrades, there's easy tool-less access to the SSD and RAM slots, which is a nice feature on a laptop. The keyboard features plenty of RGB backlit lighting that is configurable through Asus's Armory Crate software, along with an RGB light bar along the bottom of the laptop chassis, casting a distinctive glow on your desk that can sync with your keyboard and peripheral lighting.
For video connectivity, there's 1 x HDMI 2.1 port and 2 x Thunderbolt 5 ports, plus an Ethernet port for wired network access, with wireless options including Bluetooth and WiFi 7.
So if you want a ready-to-go gaming setup that's powerful enough to play all the latest game titles on a sharp 2.5K screen at high settings and frame rates, then the Asus ROG Strix G18 with RTX 5080 is a great choice, especially when you can save a hefty $600 off the price tag.

articles.title: Google says some Pixel phone owners were hacked in zero-day attacks | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Google says that a bug in its Pixel smartphones’ software was exploited in limited and targeted cyberattacks. The company said Tuesday that the bug, tracked as CVE-2026-58704, has now been patched.
According to the limited details about the vulnerability, the bug was found in Pixel phones’ modem, which lets the device connect to the internet. Exploiting the bug could allow an attacker to gain access beyond the sandboxed walls of the modem and into the broader phone’s data, a vulnerability known as privilege escalation.
The bug can be exploited silently and without any interaction from the phone owner in what’s known as a “zero-click” attack, meaning a victim does not need to click on a link or open a file.
Google did not say who was exploiting the bug, and a spokesperson for Google did not return a request for comment. It’s not uncommon for bugs like this one to be abused by surveillance vendors, such as spyware makers, who sell access to their data-stealing software to governments and law enforcement agencies.

articles.title: Assassin's Creed, Rayman, Far Cry… : Ubisoft brade tout son catalogue de jeux sur PC
articles.text:
Ubisoft a soufflé ses 40 bougies en mars, mais l’éditeur profite de la rentrée pour remettre ça avec des promotions sur sa boutique officielle. Des aventures récentes d’Assassin’s Creed aux vieux Rayman, plusieurs générations de jeux PC se retrouvent à prix vraiment intéressants.
Avant de passer commande, pensez à saisir UBI40 dans le panier. Le code retire 20 % supplémentaires des prix déjà remisés, jusqu’au 13 octobre 2026.
Quelques exceptions figurent dans les conditions de l’offre : le code ne fonctionne pas sur les précommandes, les abonnements, les monnaies virtuelles ou Assassin’s Creed Black Flag Resynced. Il ne se cumule pas non plus avec la remise fidélité obtenue en échange de vos Units.
Que faut-il acheter ?
Les plus grosses ristournes ne font pas toujours les meilleurs jeux. Voici cinq valeurs sûres du catalogue qu’on vous recommande chez Numerama.
Tous les prix ci-dessous comprennent les 20 % du code UBI40.
Watch Dogs 2 à 2 €
À 2 €, on commencerait par celui-là pour patienter avant GTA 6, toujours sans version PC annoncée. Watch Dogs 2 vous emmène dans la baie de San Francisco, où Marcus Holloway et sa bande de hackers s’en prennent aux entreprises qui surveillent les habitants.
Les possibilités sont multiples : vous pouvez survoler les lieux avec un drone, envoyer votre petit robot à roulettes pirater un équipement ou déclencher une alarme pour attirer un garde ailleurs. On peut même prendre le contrôle d’une voiture sans être au volant. Le smartphone de Marcus sert autant que ses armes, et trouver comment entrer dans un bâtiment sans y mettre les pieds devient vite un jeu en soi.
Assassin’s Creed Shadows à 22,40 €
Si vous aviez laissé passer Assassin’s Creed Shadows à sa sortie, les 22,40 € demandés ici donnent une bonne occasion de rattraper cet épisode. Comptez une quarantaine d’heures pour l’histoire principale, avec le choix de vous faufiler dans les châteaux avec Naoe ou d’en forcer l’entrée avec Yasuke.
On le recommande surtout à ceux qui rêvaient de ce détour par le Japon féodal dans cette saga. À sa sortie, ses paysages et son infiltration nous avaient particulièrement convaincus. Il faut simplement avoir encore de l’appétit pour la formule Assassin’s Creed, dont les missions restent familières et parfois redondantes.
Rayman 3: Hoodlum Havoc à 1 €
Si vous voulez mon avis, c’est ce Rayman-là qui aurait mérité un bon coup de polish, plutôt que Legends, dont le remake Retold vient d’être repoussé au 3 décembre. Sorti en 2003 sur GameCube, PS2 et Xbox, Hoodlum Havoc apportait une fraîcheur assez réjouissante avec son humour irrévérencieux et ses personnages bien allumés.
Globox avale le grand méchant, Rayman transforme ses poings en missiles téléguidés, et les Knaarens font soudain regretter l’ambiance bon enfant des premiers niveaux. Une vraie madeleine de Proust pour ceux qui l’ont connu à l’époque, et une drôle d’aventure à découvrir pour les autres. À 1 € sur PC, je reprendrais volontiers la route avec Globox.
Far Cry 6 à 4,60 €
Si vous avez encore envie de reprendre des avant-postes et de faire exploser tout ce qui passe, cet épisode a de quoi vous occuper. La formule reste familière, avec un vaste monde ouvert, des armes bricolées et une révolution à mener.
La possibilité de jouer avec un ami en coopération constitue également une très bonne raison de s’y remettre.
Avatar: Frontiers of Pandora à 13,19 €
À sa sortie, on le trouvait assez perfectible, mais l’ajout gratuit de la troisième personne, le 5 décembre 2025, lui a vraiment fait du bien.
Voir son Na’vi bondir dans la végétation et évoluer au milieu de ces décors change le plaisir de la balade. Le jeu devient bien plus contemplatif : on prend le temps de regarder la forêt s’illuminer à la nuit tombée et de s’écarter de son objectif pour explorer. À ce prix, c’est surtout une bonne affaire pour celles et ceux qui ont envie de prolonger le voyage sur Pandora après Avatar : De feu et de cendres.
Et si vous n’arrivez toujours pas à choisir, les abonnements Ubisoft+ permettent de piocher dans le catalogue. Comptez 7,99 € par mois pour Classics, consacré à une sélection d’anciens titres, ou 17,99 € par mois pour Premium, qui inclut aussi les nouveautés dès leur sortie, comme Assassin’s Creed Black Flag Resynced. Le code UBI40 ne s’applique pas à ces abonnements.

articles.title: Sony commence à corriger le gros bug audio de ses TV BRAVIA sous Android 14
articles.text:
À peine avions-nous évoqué les importants problèmes de synchronisation audio rencontrés sur plusieurs Sony BRAVIA qu’un correctif commence à être déployé. Les premiers retours sont encourageants, même si tout ne semble pas encore réglé.
Nous vous parlions hier d’un problème de synchronisation audio particulièrement gênant sur plusieurs téléviseurs Sony BRAVIA. Le défaut apparaît notamment avec des sources HDMI externes, comme une console ou un lecteur Blu-ray, lorsque le téléviseur transmet ensuite leur son à un système audio externe. Le retard peut alors s’accumuler progressivement jusqu’à atteindre plusieurs centaines de millisecondes.
Sony vient justement de commencer à déployer le firmware v114.603.100.1, disponible depuis le 14 septembre aux États-Unis et référencé au Japon depuis le lendemain. Les premiers retours d’utilisateurs indiquent que le problème de décalage audio pourrait enfin avoir été corrigé.
Sony avait bien identifié le problème
Sony avait d’ailleurs reconnu officiellement le bug sur sa page d’assistance japonaise. Le constructeur indique avoir identifié, après une mise à jour distribuée à partir du 4 juin 2026, des problèmes de synchronisation entre l’image et le son, ainsi que des bruits parasites ou micro-coupures avec certaines sources HDMI.
Sony précise qu’un correctif du problème de lip-sync est prévu courant septembre. Les modèles officiellement cités sont les A95L, BRAVIA 5, BRAVIA 7, BRAVIA 8, BRAVIA 9, BRAVIA 7 II et BRAVIA 9 II. What Hi-Fi rapporte par ailleurs des symptômes similaires sur un BRAVIA 8 II, qui ne figure pas dans cette liste officielle. Tout porte donc à croire que le firmware v114.603.100.1 correspond bien au correctif annoncé, même si son changelog reste très vague.
Tout n’est pas encore réglé
Cette mise à jour arrive après un premier correctif publié en août. Le firmware v114.602.170.1 avait notamment réglé le problème d’écran noir rencontré avec certains contenus Dolby Vision provenant d’une source HDMI externe.
Sony indique toutefois que les bruits parasites et micro-coupures audio font encore l’objet d’une investigation. Certains utilisateurs continuent également de signaler des anomalies d’affichage en Dolby Vision.
Pour les utilisateurs français, il faudra encore patienter : le firmware v114.603.100.1 n’est pas encore annoncé en Europe. Son arrivée devrait toutefois suivre prochainement si Sony conserve son calendrier habituel de déploiement.

articles.title: L Catterton to invest in restaurant chain Nandhana Foods
articles.text:
L Catterton to invest in restaurant chain Nandhana Foods
The funding by global consumer focused investment firm L Catterton is expected to support Nandhana Foods' next phase of growth.
Global consumer-focused investment firm L Catterton has entered into a definitive agreement to invest in Nandhana Foods, a leading restaurant group specialising in South Indian cuisine. The value of the investment was not disclosed.
According to a statement, the investment will support Nandhana Foods’ next phase of growth and enable the group to achieve greater scale by leveraging L Catterton’s industry expertise and operating capabilities.
L Catterton Partner Vikram Kumaraswamy said, “Nandhana Foods’ founding family has built a distinctive and scalable business with a strong consumer proposition and attractive unit economics. It has expanded the business in a disciplined manner and ensured that its restaurants remain anchored in high quality and consistency.”
He also said, “We believe there is significant headroom for additional growth by further deepening and broadening its presence in South India and penetrating other markets. There is a clear path for prudently ramping up expansion.”
Founded in 2004, Nandhana Foods is a restaurant group that specialises in Andhra and Karnataka cuisine. It operates two brands, Nandhana Palace and RNR, and has 25 branches across Bengaluru and Chennai.
Nandhana Foods Founder and Managing Director R Ravichandar said, “We are pleased to partner with L Catterton, which has a track record of creating value for its portfolio companies across the world. The firm has a profound grasp of our organisational DNA and an intricate understanding of the restaurant industry.”
The statement said L Catterton has significant experience in building restaurant brands across the world.
The firm has invested in around 30 restaurant businesses till date. Its current and past portfolio companies include Dishoom, P.F. Chang’s, Velvet Taco, Baja Fresh, Cheddar’s Scratch Kitchen, Cigierre, HUGE, Impresario, and Mendocino Farms.
Founded in 1989, L Catterton manages around $40 billion of equity capital across multi-product platforms dedicated to private equity, credit, and real estate. It has made over 300 investments in consumer brands across the world.
Edited by Swetha Kannan

articles.title: Amor y amistad con Gemini de Google: diseña juegos en pareja, sorprende con regalos y hasta comida personalizada
articles.text:
La IA se convirtió en una herramienta de uso cotidiano para organizar celebraciones, y el Día del Amor y la Amistad en Colombia no es la excepción. Gemini, el asistente de Google que emplean más de 1.000 millones de personas al mes en el mundo, ofrece funciones concretas para planificar reuniones, elegir regalos y coordinar detalles sin perder el factor sorpresa que caracteriza a esta fecha.
Cada 19 de septiembre, familias, amigos y compañeros de trabajo en distintas regiones de Colombia renuevan sus vínculos de cariño mediante reuniones, intercambios de regalos y celebraciones grupales.
PUBLICIDAD
Gemini se presenta como un recurso para acompañar ese proceso, desde la lluvia de ideas para un menú hasta la búsqueda de obsequios ajustados a un presupuesto específico o la creación de postales sonoras personalizadas.
Cómo usar Gemini para planificar el amigo secreto sin perder la sorpresa
La organización del amigo secreto suele generar dudas sobre qué comprar y cuánto gastar, en especial cuando el destinatario del regalo es alguien con quien se busca causar una buena impresión. Gemini permite resolver ese dilema mediante instrucciones detalladas que incluyen presupuesto, tipo de obsequio y hasta el contexto emocional de la situación.
PUBLICIDAD
Google compartió un ejemplo de prompt que ilustra este uso: “Gemini ayúdame a elegir el mejor regalo de amor y amistad para mi amigo secreto. Curiosamente, me salió la persona que me gusta. No quiero regalos genéricos. Para la celebración, tenemos un tope de 50.000 pesos colombianos y no quiero pasar desapercibido ni tampoco exagerar. Me estoy imaginando un regalo que contenga adentro una invitación a cenar. Dame 10 ideas de regalos y de restaurantes en los cuales pueda reservar para sorprender a mi amigo secreto”.
Este tipo de consulta muestra el nivel de personalización que admite la herramienta. En lugar de recibir una lista genérica, el usuario obtiene sugerencias ajustadas a un monto máximo, a una intención específica y a un contexto particular, como la posibilidad de combinar un obsequio físico con una invitación a un restaurante.
PUBLICIDAD
La utilidad de Gemini en este escenario radica en su capacidad para cruzar variables en simultáneo: presupuesto, gustos, tipo de vínculo y objetivo de la sorpresa. Esa combinación reduce el tiempo de búsqueda y ofrece alternativas concretas, con nombres de establecimientos y productos, en lugar de ideas abstractas.
Sugerencias de regalos personalizados según gustos y presupuesto
Uno de los usos principales que propone Google para Gemini es la generación de ideas de regalos a partir de datos concretos sobre la persona destinataria. El usuario puede compartir pistas sobre gustos, pasatiempos o preferencias, y la inteligencia artificial devuelve opciones que se ajustan a esa información.
PUBLICIDAD
Este proceso funciona como una lluvia de ideas dirigida. En lugar de recorrer tiendas físicas o catálogos extensos, la persona ingresa los datos disponibles sobre el destinatario y recibe alternativas concretas, junto con un rango de precios que respeta el presupuesto indicado.
La función resulta útil en dinámicas grupales como el amigo secreto, donde el margen de gasto suele estar definido de antemano y la presión por acertar con el regalo es mayor. Al delimitar un tope económico, como los 50.000 pesos colombianos del ejemplo mencionado, Gemini ajusta las propuestas a ese límite sin perder de vista la intención de sorprender.
PUBLICIDAD
Cómo diseñar un menú festivo con ayuda de la inteligencia artificial
Otra de las aplicaciones que destaca Google es el diseño de menús para reuniones de Amor y Amistad. Gemini permite construir propuestas gastronómicas que consideran los gustos de los invitados, sus restricciones alimenticias y el presupuesto disponible para la ocasión.
Esta función resulta relevante en encuentros donde participan personas con necesidades distintas, ya sea por alergias, preferencias vegetarianas o simplemente gustos particulares. La herramienta permite ingresar esas variables y obtener un menú coherente que evite improvisaciones de último momento.
PUBLICIDAD
El objetivo, según describe Google, es transformar una cena casual en un recuerdo especial. La planificación anticipada del menú, con ayuda de la inteligencia artificial, libera tiempo para enfocarse en otros aspectos de la organización, como la decoración o las actividades grupales.
Dinámicas y juegos interactivos generados con Gemini
La celebración de Amor y Amistad también incluye momentos de esparcimiento grupal, y Gemini puede aportar contenido original para esos espacios. Google propone usar la herramienta para inventar pistas, acertijos o coplas personalizadas inspiradas en anécdotas compartidas por el grupo de amigos o compañeros de trabajo.
PUBLICIDAD
Esta función se apoya en la capacidad de la inteligencia artificial para generar texto creativo a partir de información específica que el usuario proporciona. Al compartir detalles sobre situaciones vividas en conjunto, Gemini construye contenido que hace referencia directa a esas experiencias, lo que aporta un componente personal a los juegos.
El resultado son dinámicas que se alejan de los formatos genéricos y que incorporan referencias reconocibles solo para quienes participan del grupo. Esto refuerza el vínculo entre los asistentes y añade un elemento de humor compartido a la celebración.
PUBLICIDAD
Creación de imágenes, videos y postales sonoras para sorprender
Además de las funciones orientadas a la organización, Gemini ofrece herramientas de generación visual y sonora que permiten crear contenido único para acompañar los regalos o las felicitaciones. Google menciona la posibilidad de producir imágenes, clips de audio o videos en distintos estilos artísticos.
Esta capacidad se traduce en postales personalizadas, ilustraciones con estilos específicos o mensajes sonoros que acompañan un obsequio físico. La propuesta busca que estos elementos visuales lleven los regalos a un nivel adicional de personalización, más allá del objeto en sí mismo.
El uso de estas funciones no requiere conocimientos técnicos avanzados, ya que basta con describir el resultado deseado para que la herramienta genere una propuesta inicial. A partir de ahí, el usuario puede ajustar detalles hasta obtener el resultado que busca para su celebración de Amor y Amistad.
