articles.title: Tests de l'iPhone 18 Pro : sans surprise, le meilleur iPhone grâce à un argument — Frandroid
articles.text:
L’exercice est bien rodé : Apple présente ses nouveaux iPhone en septembre, puis la presse invitée sur place peut prendre en main les téléphones et repartir avec, pour un test complet d’une semaine. Pendant ce temps, la marque ouvre les précommandes et prépare le lancement commercial.
Après l’annonce de l’iPhone 18 Pro et l’ouverture des précommandes, voici donc la publication ce mercredi 16 septembre des tests de la presse.
En attendant le test complet de Frandroid, voici un résumé des amis de nos confrères de Numerama, Mashable, The Verge, Engadget et 9To5Mac.
Design
L’iPhone 18 Pro conserve le design introduit avec le 17 Pro et son fameux plateau photo à l’arrière. Le changement, ce sont les coloris avec un modèle rouge bordeaux et bleu glacier qui semblent plutôt séduire Engadget.
Je dois dire que j’adore les teintes « Bordeaux » et « Glacier » de mes iPhone 18 Pro et Pro Max respectivement. Mais d’après mon expérience avec l’iPhone 17 Pro couleur « burnt orange », il est sans doute bon de noter que leurs cadres en aluminium sont probablement plus sensibles aux rayures et aux éraflures que le titane de l’iPhone 16 Pro et des modèles plus anciens. Si vous êtes aussi maladroit que moi, j’ai le regret de vous le dire, mais une coque sera sans doute votre meilleure alliée.
Numerama est moins enjoué : « la teinte est sombre, un peu triste, et l’aluminium marque beaucoup plus les traces de doigts que l’orange de l’an dernier ou les couleurs « Argent » et « Glacier » de cette année. Mais il s’agit d’une question de goût ».
La vraie innovation en matière de design cette année se résume au rétrécissement de l’encoche à l’avant de 25%. Apple a fait passer le capteur infrarouge sous l’écran, et peut donc laisser plus de place à l’affichage.
Résultat, la Dynamic Island peut désormais afficher jusqu’à trois applications.
Pour 9To5Mac, malgré ce changement « Face ID fonctionne toujours aussi bien qu’avant. En plein soleil, on peut voir la caméra infrarouge sous l’écran. Sous un éclairage normal, en revanche, elle se confond parfaitement avec le reste de l’écran ».
Performances : l’énorme point fort
La grande nouveauté de l’iPhone 18 Pro, elle est sous le capot. Le téléphone intègre la nouvelle puce Apple A20 Pro, l’une des premières à utiliser le procédé 2nm de TSMC.
Un changement de procédé de fabrication permet de réduire la consommation d’une puce ou d’en augmenter les performances. Apple y associe en plus un changement d’architecture du SoC et un agrandissement de la chambre à vapeur pour le refroidissement.
Pourquoi payer la nouvelle génération au prix fort ? iPhone 17, iPhone 16 Pro et iPhone 15 Pro : trouvez le modèle parfait, révisé par des experts et garanti sur Back Market.
L’association de tous ces changements fait beaucoup de bien à l’iPhone 18 Pro. Le gap avec les précédentes générations est très impressionnant.
Mais il ne faut pas regarder que les performances CPU, la partie graphique est devenue le nerf de la guerre. C’est le GPU qui participe aux calculs liés à l’IA locale. Apple le sait, et on peut constater le travail fourni depuis plusieurs générations sur ce terrain : l’iPhone 18 Pro est plus de deux fois plus puissant que l’iPhone 16 Pro sur ce terrain (+128%).
Surtout, le refroidissement de la puce semble bien mieux maitrisé par Apple comme le relève Numerama : « au quotidien (photo intensive, navigation web, vidéo…), le 18 Pro Max chauffe visiblement moins et refroidit plus vite ».
Même son de cloche chez Mashable : « le téléphone est nettement moins chaud qu’avant. J’ai testé cela en jouant à quelques parties de PUBG: Battlegrounds avec les paramètres au maximum pendant une heure entière. Le téléphone s’est à peine réchauffé ».
Appareil Photo
L’autre grande nouveauté de l’iPhone 18 Pro : il intègre désormais un appareil photo avec un objectif à ouverture variable. Une première chez Apple, mais pas dans le monde du smartphone.
Logiciellement, la marque propose aussi beaucoup plus de réglages dans l’application Appareil Photo. Un vrai changement de philosophie pour Apple qui amuse The Verge.
Chers amis, en l’an de grâce 2026, vous pourrez enfin régler vous-mêmes les paramètres d’exposition dans l’application Appareil photo de l’iPhone. Apple a ajouté des commandes avancées pour l’ouverture mentionnée plus haut, ainsi que pour la vitesse d’obturation, la balance des blancs et la mise au point.
L’ère du « tout automatique » semble terminée, même si l’option est toujours là.
Cela ne veut pas dire que l’utilisateur lambda n’en tirera aucun avantage, mais je parie que la plupart des gens essaieront le réglage manuel de l’ouverture une seule fois, puis se contenteront de laisser l’appareil en mode automatique.
Le verdict de Mashable est sans appel : « l’iPhone 18 Pro Max dispose effectivement d’un meilleur appareil photo principal. » Le nouvel objectif peut ouvrir jusqu’à f/1,48 contre f/1,78 sur l’iPhone 17 Pro ce qui permet en principe de meilleure performances en basse lumière.
Lorsque j’ai désactivé manuellement le mode nuit, les résultats étaient nettement meilleurs sur l’iPhone 18 Pro Max : la photo présentait bien plus de détails, était globalement plus nette et comportait moins de bruit.
Pour Numerama, c’est bien la nuit que la différence se fait : « des photos de nuit vraiment meilleures » termine comme l’un des points forts de l’iPhone 18 Pro Max.
Autonomie
L’iPhone 18 Pro européen intègre une batterie de 4 056 mAh contre 3 988 mAh pour l’iPhone 17 Pro. L’iPhone 18 Pro Max passe à 5 391 mAh contre 4 823 mAh pour le 17 Pro. Avec le passage à une puce 2 nm, l’iPhone va également baisser en consommation, de quoi battre des records d’autonomie (pour un iPhone).
D’après The Verge : « je n’ai pas constaté de consommation de batterie inhabituelle sur le 18 Pro pendant mes moments de repos. Il a tenu toute une journée d’utilisation intensive lors d’un tournage vidéo sans avoir besoin d’être rechargé une seule fois, ce qui n’est pas une mince affaire ».
Mashable a aussi observé une belle autonomie : « mes tests confirment qu’Apple a considérablement amélioré l’autonomie de la batterie, qui offre désormais jusqu’à 43 heures de lecture vidéo, contre 37 sur l’iPhone 17 Pro Max ».
Attention toutefois, les iPhone américains ne proposent plus le logement pour la carte SIM physique, et peuvent donc embarquer une meilleure batterie. En Europe, Apple ne propose pas cette option, et l’on a donc une batterie plus limitée.
Pour Numerama, les premiers signes sont tout de même bons, même si un test sur une seule semaine ne permet pas de conclure définitivement.
Comme l’année dernière, nous avons passé une journée à Disneyland Paris pour tester la photo et avons terminé autour de 20 % sans la moindre recharge, là où le 17 Pro Max avait réclamé l’année dernière une batterie externe. À la mi-journée, l’iPhone 18 Pro Max affichait encore 50 %. La batterie a l’air coriace.
En revanche Numerama a été plus que séduit par un autre changement de l’iPhone, « la meilleure surprise du 18 Pro », la vitesse de recharge.
Il est maintenant possible d’obtenir plus de 50% de batterie en moins de 20 minutes et une charge complète en 1h07, sur l’iPhone 18 Pro Max, contre 1h25 jusqu’à 1h55 pour les générations précédentes.
Le prix qui pique
Malgré des gains intéressants, notamment sur les performances et l’autonomie, les journalistes restent un peu sur leurs faims à l’issue de ce test et pour une raison : la hausse de prix.
L’iPhone 18 Pro coûte 1479 euros contre 1329 euros pour son prédecesseur en 2025. Une hausse de 150 euros qui ne passe pas inapercu. Pour Engadget : « je ne pense pas que l’on en ait plus pour son argent, compte tenu du manque relatif d’améliorations par rapport aux années précédentes, où le prix d’un modèle « Pro » restait identique à celui de ses prédécesseurs ».
Conclusion
C’est une bonne façon de résumer les tests de l’iPhone 18 Pro, tous s’accordent pour dire qu’il s’agit d’une belle génération très réussie avec de vraies améliorations, notamment sur les performances, l’autonomie et la recharge.
Pour autant, ce n’est pas la génération avec le plus grand nombre de nouveautés, loin de là, et Apple y associe une belle hausse de prix qui fait grincer des dents.

articles.title: Critical ScreenConnect flaw now actively exploited in attacks
articles.text:
Attackers now exploit a critical-severity ConnectWise ScreenConnect vulnerability in the wild, according to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).
ConnectWise shared temporary mitigation measures for this missing-authorization flaw on September 7, advising security teams to disable TransferFiles permissions to block potential attacks.
The vulnerability (now tracked as CVE-2026-84869 and patched in ScreenConnect 26.6.5 and later) affects ScreenConnect clients and can let threat actors with basic privileges transfer or execute files in low-complexity attacks that don't require user interaction.
CISA added the security flaw to its catalog of actively exploited flaws on Friday and ordered U.S. federal agencies to secure their systems against ongoing attacks within three days.
"ConnectWise ScreenConnect contains both an improper privilege management and missing authorization vulnerability that may allow an attacker to file transfer and execution through an active remote sessions without authorization or host confirmation," CISA said. "These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise."
Since 2024, CISA has flagged four ScreenConnect security issues as actively exploited, two of which have also been abused in ransomware attacks.
Internet threat watchdog Shadowserver now tracks over 1,000 ScreenConnect instances still unpatched and exposed to attacks online, most of them from North America (758) and Europe (180).
ScreenConnect vulnerabilities are often targeted in the wild by both financially-motivated and state-backed hacking groups.
For instance, the North Korean-backed Kimsuky hacking group and several ransomware gangs exploited another ScreenConnect flaw (CVE-2024-1709) in 2024.
Last year, ConnectWise also rotated digital code-signing certificates after disclosing that suspected state-sponsored hackers breached its systems through code injection attacks that exploited a ViewState flaw (CVE-2025-3935) and accessed the cloud-based instances of a limited number of customers.
More recently, in March, ConnectWise addressed a cryptographic signature verification vulnerability (CVE-2026-3564) that could allow attackers to hijack unpatched ScreenConnect servers.
ConnectWise provides services to more than 100,000 IT providers worldwide, with many managed service providers (MSPs) and IT teams using its ScreenConnect remote access platform for troubleshooting, patching, and system maintenance.
Build your security blueprint for AI-powered attacks
Join Mikko Hyppönen and security leaders from the NFL, CHANEL, and Atlassian for a two-hour digital summit on what AI-speed attacks change, what defenders should stop doing, and how to validate, decide, fix, and re-validate at machine speed.

articles.title: Un agente de IA ha protagonizado un ciberataque en España. La AEPD nunca había visto uno
articles.text:
La Agencia Española de Protección de Datos (AEPD) ha recibido por primera vez la notificación de una brecha de datos personales en la que un tercero habría usado un agente de IA para ejecutar y controlar distintas fases del ataque. No se conoce la empresa que fue atacada ni qué modelo se utilizó, pero para la Agencia esta es una señal de que la amenaza teórica y potencial de la IA es ahora algo real.
Qué ha pasado. Según la información comunicada por la empresa afectada, el agente de IA comenzó buscando vulnerabilidades en archivos genéricos y logró iniciar sesión (login). Una vez dentro del sistema, continuó buscando vulnerabilidades de forma autónoma. Encontró al menos una que le permitió modificar datos personales y acceder a facturas. Hay un detalla relevante: la AEPD todavía tiene que analizar la información recibida y no explica cómo se consiguieron las credenciales para iniciar la sesión.
Esto perfila un futuro inquietante. Una agente de IA va más allá de un chatbot: no solo responde preguntas, sino que es capaz de recibir una petición para llegar a un objetivo, dividirlo en subtareas, y luego usar herramientas, ejecutar código y consultar información para decidir qué hacer a continuación.
Salto cualitativo. Eso es precisamente lo que le preocupa a la AEPD: la IA no es ya un asistente que ayuda a un ciberatacante humano, sino un atacante virtual autónomo. La agencia habla aquí de un "cambio cualitativo" en el ámbito de la ciberseguridad.
No es un caso aislado. Google advertía hace unos días de que los agentes de IA utilizados por ciberdeincuentes y grupos de espionaje están comenzando a dejar de ser experimentos para convertirse en herramientas potentísimas. Su equipo de inteligencia de amenazas ha desvelado desde grupos que usan modelos de IA para resolver problemas durante una intrusión hasta un proceso completo de robo de credenciales con múltiples agentes.
Miles de datos en seis horas. Dicha operación logró escalar privilegios y comprometer miles de credenciales en apenas seis horas. Esto supone un riesgo importante, porque los agentes pueden automatizar procesos que ya conocemos y ejecutarlos mucho más deprisa.
La IA al ataque. Esa es precisamente la preocupación que destaca la AEPD: un agente de IA puede analizar varios archivos al mismoi tiempo, probar distintas vías de entrada y modificar su estrategia según lo que encuentra. Además, si consigue una cuenta, una clave o un token con demasiados permisos, puede saltar entre servicios antes de que una empresa detecte algo anómalo.
Lo de malware se queda corto. Por eso desde la AEPD se indica que las empresas deberían icluir los ataques con agentes de IA como parte de sus análisis de riesgos. Ya no vale con tener una categoría "malware", porque este nuevo tipo de amenazas tienen una escala y se producen a una velocidad mucho mayor.
¿Cómo defendernos? La supervisión humana sigue siendo imprescindible para la Agencia, pero la seguridad ya no puede depender solo de eso. La IA había servido para demostrar que era posible detectar vulnerabilidades y corregirlas, pero con los agentes de IA que pueden usar los ciberdelincuentes, tanto la defensa como el ataque se producen ahora con una velocidad y capacidad que superan la de los expertos humanos. Desde el Centro Criptológico Nacional (CCN) se apunta a este cambio de paradigma, y se ofrece una guía de buenas prácticas para evitar estas amenazas.

articles.title: "L'IA a le potentiel de tous nous tuer" : un troisième chercheur en IA démissionne en une semaine
articles.text:
"L'IA a le potentiel de tous nous tuer" : un troisième chercheur en IA démissionne en une semaine
Après Anthropic, c'est Google DeepMind qui voit l'un de ses spécialistes de la sûreté de l'IA partir en tirant le signal d'alarme. Bilal Chughtai, ingénieur de recherche en interprétabilité des modèles et en alignement de l'AGI, estime que l'humanité est en train de manquer de temps.
Ce lundi 15 septembre, Bilal Chughtai, ancien ingénieur de recherche chez Google DeepMind spécialisé en sûreté de l'intelligence artificielle générale (AGI), a publié sur X un message glaçant. Diplômé de Cambridge, co-auteur de travaux sur l'interprétabilité des réseaux de neurones, Chughtai avait quitté Google en juillet 2026. Son alerte vient ponctuer une séquence d'une violence rare dans l'histoire de l'IA.
	
Je crois sincèrement que l'IA a le potentiel de tous nous tuer, et que nous sommes peut-être en train de manquer de temps pour éviter cette issue.
I recently resigned from Google DeepMind, where I worked on AGI safety and alignment research. At Google, I witnessed AI development first hand. I too am extremely concerned by the default trajectory of this technology. I earnestly believe that AI has the potential to kill us…
— bilal 🔶 (@bilalchughtai_) September 14, 2026
Démissions en série et aveux publics chez Anthropic
Tout a commencé le 9 septembre. Jacob Coxon, 27 ans, chercheur ayant travaillé chez OpenAI puis Anthropic, a annoncé sa démission sur X dans un post vu plus de 100 millions de fois. "Les gens qui construisent l'IA croient sincèrement qu'elle pourrait tous nous tuer d'ici la fin de la décennie", a-t-il écrit, précisant qu'il partait deux mois avant l'acquisition de ses stock-options.
Quelques heures plus tard, Evan Hubinger, responsable de la recherche en alignement chez Anthropic et toujours en poste, a surenchéri publiquement : il estime à plus de 10 % la probabilité que l'IA provoque l'extinction de l'humanité dans les dix prochaines années. Et concède qu'Anthropic "n'a pas encore de plan pour résoudre l'alignement de la superintelligence".
Amodei appelle à freiner, Altman et Musk suivent
Le 12 septembre, Dario Amodei, PDG d'Anthropic, a publié un essai de près de 4 000 mots intitulé We Must Pace the Frontier. Il y appelle l'industrie à ralentir délibérément le rythme d'amélioration des modèles, estimant que des agents d'IA autonomes pourraient s'emparer d'internet en six mois. Il invoque deux déclencheurs : l'accélération de l'auto-amélioration récursive des systèmes d'IA, et un incident survenu en juillet au cours duquel un essaim d'agents autonomes propulsés par un modèle d'OpenAI a mené des cyberattaques hors de son périmètre assigné.
Sam Altman (OpenAI), Demis Hassabis (Google DeepMind) et Elon Musk (xAI) ont aussitôt soutenu cet appel. Convergence rarissime. Donald Trump, lui, a balayé l'ensemble sur les réseaux sociaux en un mot : "hoax".

articles.title: AI uncovers hidden Ozempic side effects across 400,000 Reddit posts
articles.text:
AI uncovers hidden Ozempic side effects across 400,000 Reddit posts
AI analysis of 400,000 Reddit posts uncovered potentially overlooked symptoms reported by users of Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, and Zepbound.
- Date:
- September 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of Pennsylvania School of Engineering and Applied Science
- Summary:
- AI analysis of 400,000 Reddit posts found that users of drugs such as Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, and Zepbound reported unexpected symptoms including menstrual changes, chills, hot flashes, and fatigue. Researchers cannot say the medications caused these problems, but the patterns may reveal overlooked signals worth studying.
- Share:
Artificial intelligence is giving researchers a new way to listen to what patients are saying about popular GLP-1 drugs. After analyzing more than 400,000 Reddit posts, a University of Pennsylvania team identified several symptoms reported by people using semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy, and Rybelsus) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro and Zepbound) that may not be fully represented in clinical trials or official regulatory information.
The study, published recently in Nature Health, examined more than five years of posts from nearly 70,000 Reddit users. Two categories stood out as particularly deserving of further investigation: reproductive symptoms, including changes in menstrual cycles, and problems involving body temperature, such as chills and hot flashes.
The findings do not establish that the medications caused these symptoms. Instead, researchers say the massive collection of spontaneous patient reports may reveal signals worth examining more closely.
"Some of the side effects we found, like nausea, are well known, and that shows that the method is picking up a real signal," says Sharath Chandra Guntuku, Research Associate Professor in Computer and Information Science (CIS) at Penn Engineering and the study's senior author. "The underreported symptoms are leads that came from patients themselves, unprompted, and clinicians could potentially pay attention to them."
What Patients Report Outside Clinical Trials
Clinical trials are designed to determine whether treatments work and to identify important safety problems, but they cannot necessarily capture every symptom that matters to patients once a medication is being used by a much larger population.
"Clinical trials generally identify the most dangerous side effects of drugs," adds Lyle Ungar, Professor in CIS and a co-author on the study. "But they can fail to find what symptoms patients are most concerned about; even though social media is not necessarily representative, a large collection of posts may reflect additional concerns."
The distinction is important. The study found associations in what people discussed online, not proof that GLP-1 drugs were responsible for those experiences.
"We can't say that GLP-1s are actually causing these symptoms," notes Neil Sehgal, the study's first author and a doctoral student in CIS advised by Guntuku and Ungar. "But nearly 4% of the Reddit users in our sample reported menstrual irregularities, which would be even higher in a female-only sample. We think that's a signal worth investigating."
Using Social Media as an Early Health Signal
The idea of mining online conversations for clues about drug safety predates today's AI boom. In 2011, Ungar participated in one of the earliest efforts to use material created by internet users to identify possible adverse effects from medications.
Social media can capture experiences that patients discuss with one another but may never formally report to a doctor, drug manufacturer, or regulator.
"Online patient communities work a lot like a neighborhood grapevine," says Ungar. "People who are living with these medications are swapping notes with each other in real time, sharing experiences that rarely make it into a doctor's office visit or an official report."
Since then, online patient communities have expanded enormously. That has made social media a potentially valuable source for studying how medications affect people in everyday life, although gaining access to platform data has become more difficult.
Traditional clinical research remains essential, the researchers emphasize, but online conversations can provide information far more quickly when millions of people begin using a drug.
"Clinical trials are the gold standard, but by design, they are slow," says Guntuku. "This is not a replacement for trials, but it can move much faster, and that speed matters when a drug goes from niche to mainstream almost overnight."
AI Makes Massive Social Media Analysis Possible
One of the biggest obstacles has always been scale.
Guntuku describes the approach as "computational social listening," which uses computational methods to identify patterns in large collections of online conversations about health.
Patients, however, rarely describe symptoms using standardized medical terminology. One person might describe feeling unusually cold, another might mention constant chills, while a clinician could categorize those experiences using a specific medical term.
Researchers therefore need a way to translate everyday language into standardized categories. One important reference is the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA), which provides terminology widely used to classify medical conditions, symptoms, and adverse events.
Previously, connecting huge numbers of informal social media posts with standardized medical terminology required enormous amounts of work, limiting how much data researchers could realistically analyze.
Large language models such as GPT and Gemini are changing that equation by allowing researchers to process and categorize vast amounts of text more consistently and quickly.
"Large language models have made it possible to do this kind of analysis much faster with a level of standardization that could be difficult to achieve before," says Sehgal.
Unexpected Symptoms Emerge From 400,000 Posts
The researchers stress that Reddit users do not represent the overall population of people taking GLP-1 drugs. Reddit users tend to be younger, are more likely to be male, and are disproportionately located in the United States.
Even with that limitation, the analysis produced a reassuring sign that the approach was detecting genuine patterns. Many of the symptoms discussed by Reddit users closely matched already known effects of semaglutide and tirzepatide.
About 44% of users included in the study described at least one side effect. Gastrointestinal problems were the most common, consistent with the nausea and other digestive issues already associated with these medications.
More intriguing were symptoms that appeared frequently enough to attract the researchers' attention but may not be as well represented in current drug labels or conventional adverse event reports.
Nearly 4% of users who reported side effects described reproductive symptoms. These included changes in menstruation such as bleeding between periods, heavy bleeding, and irregular menstrual cycles.
Users also described changes involving body temperature, including chills, feeling unusually cold, hot flashes, and symptoms resembling a fever.
Fatigue was another notable finding. It was the second most frequently reported complaint in the Reddit data, even though relatively few clinical trials reported fatigue often enough for it to reach established reporting thresholds.
Why Menstrual and Temperature Changes Are Interesting
One possible reason these reports caught researchers' attention involves the hypothalamus, a small but extremely important region of the brain. Among its many jobs, the hypothalamus helps regulate hunger, hormones, reproduction and body temperature.
"These drugs are thought to work by engaging part of the brain called the hypothalamus, which helps regulate a wide variety of hormones," says Jena Shaw Tronieri, Senior Research Investigator at Penn's Center for Weight and Eating Disorders and a co-author of the study. "That doesn't mean the medications are necessarily causing these symptoms, but it could suggest that reports of menstrual changes and body temperature fluctuations are worth studying more systematically."
The researchers are not proposing that this biological connection proves GLP-1 drugs are responsible. Instead, it offers another reason to test the patient-reported patterns more carefully through controlled research.
Turning Online Conversations Into Research Leads
For now, the team hopes the results encourage scientists and clinicians to pay closer attention to symptoms that patients repeatedly discuss online.
"They're clearly on patients' minds, and that's worth paying attention to," says Sehgal.
The researchers also want to broaden their analysis beyond Reddit and beyond English-language communities. Doing so could help determine whether the same patterns emerge among different groups of people and on different social media platforms.
"We don't really know yet whether what we're seeing on Reddit reflects the experience of GLP-1 users globally, or whether it's particular to the kind of person who posts on Reddit in the United States," Ungar says.
In the longer term, rapid AI analysis of online patient conversations could potentially become an early detection system for emerging health concerns involving drugs, supplements and wellness products.
That could be particularly valuable for substances that become popular online faster than conventional research can keep up. Loosely regulated or unregulated products, including injectable peptides, can spread quickly through communities on Reddit, TikTok and other platforms. Discussions among users may therefore provide some of the earliest indications of unexpected effects.
"The whole point of this kind of approach is that it can move quickly, and that's exactly when it's most valuable," says Guntuku.
This study was conducted at the University of Pennsylvania School of Engineering and Applied Science. The authors report no outside funding. Tronieri reports receiving an investigator-initiated grant, on behalf of the University of Pennsylvania, from Novo Nordisk and receiving consulting fees from Currax Pharmaceuticals, LLC. The other authors report no conflicts of interest.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Pennsylvania School of Engineering and Applied Science. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Neil K. R. Sehgal, Jena Shaw Tronieri, Lyle Ungar, Sharath Chandra Guntuku. Self-reported side effects of semaglutide and tirzepatide in online communities. Nature Health, 2026; 1 (8): 806 DOI: 10.1038/s44360-026-00108-y

articles.title: TIM pode acabar com TIM Beta; novos planos estão a caminho • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
TIM pode acabar com TIM Beta; novos planos estão a caminho
Programa batizado de BetaCreator dependerá de convite. Novas definições devem ser feitas nas próximas semanas.
O Tecnoblog apurou que o TIM Beta deve passar por uma grande reformulação, inclusive com mudança de nome para BetaCreator. A operadora de origem italiana está prestes a enviar os convites para que mais clientes participem da iniciativa.
Criado em 2011, o TIM Beta foi, por anos, um dos serviços de telefonia mais bem falados do país, por trazer a economia do pré-pago com a mecânica de gamificação a partir de tarefas, em especial nas redes sociais.
De acordo com a TIM, a reformulação “busca atualizar esse conceito para uma nova geração de consumidores, preservando elementos que marcaram a trajetória do Beta, como a exclusividade, o senso de pertencimento e a construção de comunidade”. A empresa confirmou com exclusividade ao Tecnoblog que o novo BetaCreator vai depender de convites. Ou seja, não será possível simplesmente aderir à novidade.
E quais são os novos planos e preços? Nós ainda não sabemos. Eu levei esses questionamentos à equipe da TIM e fui informado de que as ofertas, franquias e benefícios serão construídos “em conjunto com as pessoas que entrarem nessa primeira fase”. A ideia é ter uma abordagem mais colaborativa, algo em alta em inúmeros setores, não apenas o de telefonia.
Os primeiros passos em direção ao novo BetaCreator foram dados no Rock in Rio. Patrocinadora do festival, a TIM promoveu a degustação da rede 5G por meio de eSIMs ofertados gratuitamente. Um balanço divulgado hoje (15/09) mostrou que o evento movimentou quase 200 TB de dados e atingiu pico de 44 mil conexões simultâneas na rede da TIM.
De fato, pouco se sabe sobre o BetaCreator. Eu apurei que, passado o Rock in Rio, novas informações devem ser divulgadas nas próximas semanas. A TIM ainda vai definir o futuro dos atuais clientes do TIM Beta – eles permanecerão nos planos atuais ou serão migrados?
Hoje, o TIM Beta oferece franquia de até 30 GB por R$ 60 mensais, segundo o site da TIM. Ele conta com acesso sem custo adicional à plataforma de música Deezer na modalidade Premium. O serviço está dividido entre os planos Beta, Lab e Lab+.
Este é apenas um dos movimentos recentes da prestadora, que também entrou no streaming com o TIM Play e trabalha no desenvolvimento de uma função contra telemarketing, nos moldes do que foi feito, de forma pioneira, pela Vivo, e agora também foi anunciado pela Claro.

articles.text:
StarCraft creative director says the game and the real-world feel 'very close in terms of themes and characters' — 'When you look at the stories that were told in StarCraft and the characters that you run into, it's remarkably topical'
Dan Hay says it's "remarkable" how StarCraft "translates quite easily into today"
- StarCraft general manager and creative director Dan Hay says the series' stories and characters are "remarkably topical" today
- Hay says StarCraft and the real world are both like a "frontier"
- He adds that while StarCraft is science fiction, its "themes and characters" are very similar to "the headlines in our world"
StarCraft general manager and creative director Dan Hay has compared real-world events to the series' stories and characters, calling them "remarkably topical."
In a sit-down interview with TechRadar Gaming following the reveal of StarCraft, a first-person, open-world shooter slated to arrive in 2030, Hay discussed the CGI trailer that debuted at BlizzCon and explained that the team wanted to portray the "tension" that will come with this new story-driven adventure.
The developer also said that building the "stakes" was just as important; he couldn't dive too much into the narrative details, but Hay touched on the series as a whole and its storylines that explore "imperfect" characters, suggesting the new StarCraft will examine similar topics.
"The way in which you are a hero is that you are going to learn how to become one," Hay said. "The way in which you are a hero is that you are going to learn how to become one. So it's not perfect, right? And that's the thing about StarCraft: a lot of the characters are not perfect; they're imperfect, and even the villains are.
"They have an idea of what you think they are at the beginning of the game, and then by the end of the game, you realize, oh, they were something completely different. And I think what's powerful about StarCraft."
Hay continued, saying that when you look at StarCraft's stories and the characters you meet, they're "remarkably topical" to the events unfolding in the real world.
"When you think about our world today, and you think about what is StarCraft? It's a bit of a frontier," he said. "It's obviously a frontier. There's asymmetry in terms of factions that don't agree with each other. There's brinkmanship going on where one faction is being used against another. [In] a lot of cases, it's just over resources.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
"A lot of the cases there's politics, and there's intrigue, and there are people being left behind and betrayed, and when you look at that, and then you look at the headlines in our world, it's not super far [apart] in terms of how it feels sometimes. So you feel that tension, and you felt that tension in the teaser [trailer]."
Hay concluded: "I think what's remarkable about StarCraft is that it feels real, and it feels like it translates quite easily into today. And even though it's science fiction, and even though it has this sense of being in this other universe, it feels very close in terms of themes and characters and moments that you could experience today."

articles.title: NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 Delivers Leading Performance in MLPerf Inference v6.1 Debut
articles.text:
System performance, efficient infrastructure scaling and continuous software optimization are key levers that determine AI inference economics. Higher system performance means more tokens generated, resulting in higher revenue. Efficient scaling means throughput grows proportionally as hardware gets added, requiring fewer resources to serve users at scale. Continuous optimization means generating more value from infrastructure investments.
Underlying all three is platform fungibility: the same infrastructure runs any model, any workload, from training to inference, recommender to reasoning, language to video, keeping utilization high.
The NVIDIA platform is purpose-built to optimize across all these, as highlighted by MLPerf Inference v6.1 results released today:
- NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 system debuts with leading performance: In its first MLPerf Inference preview submission, NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 delivers up to 3.7x better throughput than GB300 NVL72.
- NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 scales with leading efficiency: A 288-GPU submission across four GB300 NVL72 racks achieved 99% scaling efficiency, with throughput growing nearly linearly from a single-rack baseline.
- Continuous software optimizations drive performance gains: Software optimizations in NVIDIA’s MLPerf Inference v6.1 submissions delivered up to 1.6x higher performance over v6.0. Optimizations continued post-v6.1 submission, delivering further performance gains.
For organizations making AI infrastructure decisions, performance, scaling efficiency and software velocity are important considerations that determine long-term inference economics.
Vera Rubin NVL72 Makes MLPerf Inference Debut With Leading Performance
NVIDIA submitted Vera Rubin NVL72 preview results on two of the most demanding benchmarks in the MLPerf Inference v6.1 suite: DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen3-VL.
Vera Rubin NVL72 delivers up to 3.7x higher throughput than GB300 NVL72 on Qwen3-VL across offline, server and interactive scenarios, using vLLM with the NVIDIA Dynamo open source inference framework. On DeepSeek-R1, using the NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM library, throughput is up to 2.5x higher than GB300 NVL72. These early results showcase NVIDIA’s accelerated pace of innovation and how performance will improve with continuous software optimizations.
This performance means each Vera Rubin NVL72 rack delivers significantly more tokens, serves more users and generates more revenue than a GB300 NVL72 rack, while lowering cost per token.
The results reflect full-stack codesign across hardware and software. Vera Rubin’s enhanced Tensor Cores and Transformer Engine accelerate both the prefill and decode stages of inference, while NVFP4 precision reduces memory footprint across model weights, attention and KV cache — increasing throughput with minimal loss of output quality.
Vera Rubin submissions heavily used disaggregated serving, separating prefill and decode along with large-scale expert parallelism for maximum efficiency across the mixture-of-experts layers that power models like DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen3-VL.
The NVL72 scale-up domain — powered by sixth-generation NVIDIA NVLink and NVLink Switch to deliver 10x higher packet rates and 3x lower latency than off-the-shelf Ethernet — provides the interconnect foundation that makes these techniques effective at rack scale.
This codesign extends to NVIDIA’s partner ecosystem: Nebius also submitted Vera Rubin NVL72 preview results and demonstrated excellent performance.
AI agents, which reason, plan and act across multiple steps, are reshaping how inference performance is measured. In benchmarks designed to capture this shift, such as SemiAnalysis AgentX, Vera Rubin NVL72 delivered 30x better performance than GB300 NVL72 in preview testing. In addition, the upcoming MLPerf Endpoints benchmark will bring standardized measurement to agentic inference workloads, beyond what traditional throughput benchmarks capture.
NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 Scales With Leading Efficiency
Scaling efficiency — how effectively additional GPUs translate to throughput gains — is a key measure of AI infrastructure productivity. NVIDIA delivers this with high-bandwidth, low-latency scale-up interconnects within each rack, high-bandwidth networking between racks and efficient request orchestration across nodes.
NVIDIA’s DeepSeek-R1 (DSR1) submission scaled from a single GB300 NVL72 rack (72 GPUs) to four racks (288 GPUs), achieving 99% scaling efficiency in the offline scenario. Throughput grew nearly in proportion to the hardware added.
Scaling efficiency is key because more GPUs don’t automatically mean proportionally more throughput. If adding nearly double the GPU count delivered only a single-digit percentage improvement in throughput, the infrastructure cost would far outpace the performance return. The architecture, interconnect and software must all scale together.
GB300 NVL72 also demonstrated rack-scale efficiency on the WAN 2.2 text-to-video benchmark, reaching 0.65 720p videos per second at 5.7 seconds per video — 9x higher throughput and 7.5x lower latency than a single node.
Software Optimizations Drive Continuous Gains
NVIDIA platform undergoes continuous software development, delivering performance and feature improvements.
In v6.1, GB300 NVL72 performance on Qwen3-VL improved up to 1.6x over v6.0 results. The gains came through lower KV cache precision, additional kernel fusion, better kernels and disaggregated serving with vLLM and NVIDIA Dynamo.
Software optimization continued past the v6.1 submission deadline as well. Post-submission results, not yet verified by MLCommons, on GPT-OSS-120B and DLRMv3 show further performance gains.
AI Inference at Every Scale
Beyond the NVIDIA Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin NVL72 platform results, NVIDIA submitted Jetson AGX Thor results using NVIDIA TensorRT Edge-LLM on the newly introduced Edge-Agentic benchmark with Qwen3.6-27B.
The NVIDIA partner ecosystem participated broadly, with 19 partners — eight of them on multi-node Blackwell NVL72 systems — demonstrating excellent performance. This includes ASUS, Azure, Cisco, CoreWeave, Crusoe, Dell Technologies, Fujitsu, Giga Computing, HPE, Inventec, Lambda, MiTAC Computing, Nebius, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, Quanta Cloud Technology, Red Hat, ScitiX, Supermicro and Wiwynn.
From compact edge devices to the largest AI factories, NVIDIA continues to advance performance across the full technology stack with an annual cadence of platform architectures, continuously improving software and an ecosystem built to deliver it at scale.
Learn more about the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform.

articles.title: The iPhone 18 Pro’s big camera update is all about the small gains
articles.text:
Last week, Apple announced an iPhone unlike any it has made in the past. An iPhone that has seemingly already led several other phone manufacturers to pursue entirely different designs for their flagship products. A remarkably distinct device with the kind of “I can’t believe they did that” software touches that Apple sometimes pulls off when it’s at the top of its game.
The iPhone 18 Pro’s big camera update is all about the small gains
The Pro camera’s major upgrade offers minor image quality improvements — whether or not you know what an f-stop is.
If you buy something from a Verge link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
That phone is not the iPhone 18 Pro.
The 18 Pro and Pro Max are in the unusual position of being the second-most interesting iPhones that Apple is launching this year. The foldable iPhone Duo stole the show at Apple’s launch event, but it’s not arriving until next month. In the meantime, the 18 Pro cometh, and it is extremely familiar even with a totally new hardware feature in the camera.
It is so similar to the iPhone 17 Pro that it can use the same cases. Have you used an iPhone 17 Pro? Great, you now know what it’s like to use the 18 Pro. There are no surprises, and unless you’re a truly committed smartphone photographer, no hugely compelling reason to pick an 18 Pro over a 17 Pro if you can find one on sale. It’s what we’ve come to expect from what was the flagship iPhone: excellent and utterly iterative.
Apple iPhone 18 Pro
The Good
- Manual exposure controls in the native camera app, finally
- Marginal improvements to image quality
- Photographing sunstars with a smartphone camera rules
The Bad
- $100 more expensive than last year
- Manual exposure controls are tiny
- Higher storage tiers are quite pricey
The Good
- Manual exposure controls in the native camera app, finally
- Marginal improvements to image quality
- Photographing sunstars with a smartphone camera rules
The Bad
- $100 more expensive than last year
- Manual exposure controls are tiny
- Higher storage tiers are quite pricey
Inside, the iPhone 18 Pro has a revamped thermal management design that allows its new A20 Pro chip to sustain full performance for longer, but the biggest truly new idea is inside the main camera, where Apple has added a moving aperture to control how much light hits the sensor. This is a big deal, and also a small deal, which I promise makes sense.
With a few exceptions, phone cameras have fixed apertures. Their sensors and lenses are so small that most of your scene is in focus even when you’re shooting wide open, and it’s usually best to get as much light as you can on that tiny sensor anyway. But there are some edge cases where a narrower aperture is helpful, even on a phone camera. It could also be helpful in other situations, particularly in low light, to open up the aperture even further than the iPhone’s traditional f/1.8. So Apple seems to have said, “Screw it. Let’s have it both ways,” and put in a variable aperture.
So there are really two separate things happening here. The maximum aperture is now bigger, at f/1.48 vs. f/1.8, and has the ability to get smaller, with stops available at f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4. And while both the larger and smaller apertures do offer marginal improvements to photo quality in some cases, the differences are generally marginal.
One of the reasons photographers like a wider aperture is for its ability to throw more of the background of a photo out of focus. But the small lens and sensor on a smartphone camera don’t allow for the same kind of soft background blur you get from a bigger camera system. At the iPhone’s old maximum aperture of f/1.8, most things are in focus most of the time, and going to the slightly wider f/1.48 doesn’t make a huge difference.
A bigger aperture does offer an advantage for low light photography. On a traditional camera, letting in more light allows the system to keep noise down by using a faster shutter speed, a lower ISO, or both. It’s not quite the same on a smartphone camera that’s combining multiple frames at different exposures to create the final image, but broadly the concept of “more light = better photo” holds.
Maybe because phones are already so good at coping with low light through these computational methods, the low light gains in the 18 Pro look pretty minor. If I look closely at the detail in a shot at f/1.48 versus f/1.8, I can see a difference, but it’s subtle.
The biggest advantage might be for Night Mode. At f/1.48, the system can use a slightly shorter Night Mode capture time compared to f/1.8. That’s less time you have to try and keep your hand still and less noise that the system needs to try and process out.
On the other side of the dial, a smaller aperture is useful for extending depth of field and keeping more stuff in focus, particularly if your subject is close to the camera. If you’re taking a close-up photo of a statue, at f/1.48 or f/1.8 the back part of it might look a bit soft. Stopping down to f/4 sharpens up the part in the background.
That’s helpful! But once again, you’ll find these benefits on the margins. That’s because the iPhone’s new f/1.48 maximum aperture actually equates to about f/5 on full frame in terms of depth of field, which already puts a lot of the stuff in front of and behind your subject in focus. Unless you’re really close to your subject, most things are in focus or close enough when you photograph them with a smartphone camera.
If you don’t know or care about f-stops, you’ll still get along just fine with this updated camera. By default the aperture is set to automatically adjust based on lighting conditions, and it seems to stay at f/1.8 most of the time in good lighting. The aperture does open up to f/1.48 in dim light automatically, and will close down to f/4 when taking a group photo with someone who’s standing further back. And I saw it consistently dropping down to f/4 when I was taking a photo of some close-up text. That’s a situation where f/4 will help you get more in focus and make for a potentially more usable photo. But that’s an awfully narrow set of use cases, whether you’re the kind of person who wants to take manual control over the aperture or not.
That’s the big update, and the effect is a relatively small one. But it’s not the only camera update. Friends, in the year of our Lord 2026, you can finally change the exposure controls by yourself in the iPhone camera app. Apple has added pro controls for the aforementioned aperture as well as shutter speed, white balance, and focus. There’s also the exposure compensation control that existed before, though no direct ISO adjustment, which someone coming from a traditional camera system would probably look for. But there’s enough control here for anyone who is so inclined to get a little more creative and hands-on with the stock app than ever before.
I noticed that when I was using a manual shutter speed, the results appeared to have been less processed. Apple spokesperson Stephanie Ng confirmed that the camera is indeed capturing a single frame rather than using the typical multi-frame processing. That means you lose a bit of dynamic range, though the final image will still include a gain map if there are highlights bright enough to warrant it. That’s not ideal if you’re trying to capture detail in both highlights and shadows, but on the other hand, this is one way to get the less-processed iPhone photo that some folks have been clamoring for. It’s a bit hidden, but it’s finally here.
On top of that, there’s a new set of texture controls for Photographic Styles, with the ability to add a film-inspired glow to highlight areas of your photo, overlay film grain, or soften skin. It’s another first for Apple: the ability to make your photos a little bit worse. But you know, tastefully, Film simulation modes for digital cameras are as popular as ever, and Apple is trying to catch that wave. The recently released Pixel 11 series includes so many ways to customize the look of your photos that their camera team had an escalation meeting about it. Likewise, Samsung has added any number of ways you can restyle your photo into what you envisioned it would be. After basically a decade of pushing the technological envelope year after year, the major phone manufacturers seem to be opening up to other definitions of image quality.
If you put all these updates together alongside the less-important but completely underrated addition of a first-party wrist strap (!) accessory for Apple’s own 18 Pro cases, maybe there’s something more camera than phone here. When I got my hands on the 18 Pro last week, I wondered if I could convince myself that the iPhone is a camera camera now.
I will go so far as to say that I had a better time shooting with the 18 Pro than I’ve ever had using an iPhone camera in the past. I shot sunstars peeking out behind some leaves in Battery Park. I took it to the US Open and documented the excitement of a night match at Arthur Ashe Stadium. I took a video of a sizzling fajita plate and converted it to a cinematic masterpiece* after capture. But I never forgot I was using a phone. The pro control icons are pretty small on the 18 Pro’s screen, and I had to focus just to hit them properly. I had to dismiss a spam call in the middle of a shoot. And after a morning of battery-draining photo and video shooting, it became really important to top the battery off so as not to lose my lifeline to the rest of the world. It’s a step closer, and the moving aperture is a bit closer to that dream of a phone that’s also a camera. But it’s still a phone.
*I use the term masterpiece loosely.
Apple, Google, and Samsung have each achieved their own kind of excellence in shaping what a smartphone camera can be. So it’s interesting watching them pivot to flexibility and embracing some of the flaws that are turning people on to old digital cameras. But taking photos with one of their flagship phones still feels like using a phone, whether there are moving aperture blades inside or not. One of the reasons I found the wrist strap so appealing was that it made the process of handling the phone as a camera feel more like, well, a camera. I’m hoping for the day when one of the few phone makers who sell devices in the US at scale tries something like the Xiaomi photography kits or Vivo’s telephoto lenses. That would feel like a whole new camera experience.
Apple is also using the 18 Pro to introduce something it calls Reference Image, which is a method the company has developed for verifying the authenticity of a photo taken on the iPhone. Apple will start using Google’s SynthID standard to tag photos with AI edits, but Reference Image comes at the problem from the other direction: helping people to identify which photos are real. Apple designed a new main camera sensor for the 18 Pro and Pro Max that adds encrypted data to the images it produces, so it’s limited to photos taken with the main camera on those two models. It’s complicated and clunky right now, but it also seems to be a pretty robust system with a lot of room to grow.
You need to enable it as a camera mode in the settings app in order to use it, and then actively switch the camera app to Reference mode to capture a Reference Image. The resulting image file contains the encrypted data from the main sensor, which means it’s bigger than a normal photo — a standard 4MB image I shot of a city street is an 8MB file when I shoot it in reference mode. If you send a Reference Image to someone who wants to verify that a Reference Image hasn’t been tampered with, they can push a button to send it to Apple’s Private Cloud Compute, where that encrypted data will be “developed” showing the image basically as it came off the sensor. (Apple’s metaphor here is having the original negative of a traditional film photograph.)
It’s hard to use at the moment, but the idea is that it’s almost impossible to tamper with. Apple is releasing an API for third-party developers to add an option to view reference photos when they’re attached to an image, and the company seems eager to push this into the wider ecosystem now that all of this has been announced.
There are some meaningful updates on the video side of the aisle, too. There’s updated focus tracking that uses AI to stick to a subject. It’ll even pick them up if they leave the frame briefly and come back, but in my brief testing it seems to forget about someone if they’re gone for more than a few seconds. You can also convert video footage from the main camera to Cinematic after the fact, in the same way that you can convert regular photos to portrait mode after you take them. I often wish I’d taken video in cinematic mode but I never remember to in the moment, so this is a nice update. Video files don’t appear to be vastly bigger compared to similar clips from the 17 Pro, so this doesn’t come at a big cost to your storage space, either.
And that’s no small thing. The 18 Pro and Pro Max are each $100 more this year, with the 18 Pro starting at $1,199 with 256GB of storage. But each jump in storage tier will cost you dearly — all the way up to a $2,399 version for 2TB. Likewise, the Pro Max starts at $1,299.99 with 256GB of storage and goes all the way up to $2,499 for the 2TB version.
You’re not getting nothing for that price hike. There’s a new chipset, the A20 Pro, plus an updated vapor chamber that’s supposed to move heat away from the chipset more effectively to help with sustained performance compared to the 17 Pro. I noted the phone getting pretty warm on my first few days of using it, which are usually pretty taxing as you’re going through setup, app downloads, and data indexing, but haven’t noticed it as a consistent problem.
Battery life is the eternally impossible question to answer about a phone after a week of using it. I haven’t experienced anything like a “normal day” for the past week, but I haven’t seen any surprising battery drain from the 18 Pro in my downtime, either. It survived a day of intense use during a video shoot without a recharge at any point, which is no small feat. Apple quotes a modest gain in battery life for the smaller Pro model — 36 hours of video playback, up from 33 hours on the 17 Pro. The 18 Pro Max offers a bigger increase: 45 hours of video playback compared to 39 on the 17 Pro Max. Verge editor-in-chief Nilay Patel has been testing the Pro Max, and he says it’s been lasting more than a day, although he also noted the same early setup vibes. He also points out his 17 Pro Max battery was a champ when it was new and now can’t make it through a day after a year of heavy use, so the real test here is going to come much later in this phone’s life cycle.
The real test here is going to come much later in this phone’s life cycle
The 18 Pro I’m testing uses Apple’s new in-house C2 modem, marking the first time that a Pro iPhone has shipped with an Apple-made cellular chip. It seems that the homegrown stuff has finally cleared Apple’s quality bar for inclusion at the very high end, and I can’t say I’ve found any reason to fault it over the past week. The C2 is paired with the N1 wireless networking chip, and the system overall seems quick to jump off a Wi-Fi signal when I’m in an elevator and just as eager to pick up a cell signal when I step out. Here’s hoping it’s just as quick to ditch my home Wi-Fi when I’m in the carport outside of my house trying to start GPS navigation — truly, the dream.
One other notable update here is that the Dynamic Island is smaller. On the 17 Pro, the black bar encompassed the Face ID sensor in addition to the front-facing camera. On the 18 Pro, the Face ID sensor is hidden under the regular part of the screen until that real estate is needed by the Dynamic Island. Apple went to great lengths to disguise the sensor under a unique pixel pattern that uses black pixels to allow the IR signals necessary for Face ID to pass through. Pretty cool, though I can’t say I noticed the Dynamic Island’s smaller size even a single time as I was using the phone, and jumping back to the 17 Pro’s larger Dynamic Island hasn’t bothered me. And I have yet to need three items in the Dynamic Island at one time, rather than two, but this is a new capability that exists on the 18 Pro.
Possibly an even bigger deal than the launch of a new $1,200 phone is the release of iOS 27, and with it the new-new AI Siri. We previewed it in detail earlier this summer, and it continues to impress me. Particularly, its ability to search across email and messages all at once — this keeps feeling more and more like a superpower the longer I use it. We also noted when it debuted that Siri as an AI chatbot is much less chatty and eager to keep you engaged than the likes of Gemini or ChatGPT, which is something I also appreciate the more I use it. iOS 27 has just gone fully public this week, and it will be interesting to see how people take to the new Siri. It has a lot of work to do to earn the trust of the public that it can do anything more complex than setting a timer reliably, but Siri seems to be on the right track at least. Finally.
Unlike Siri, the 18 Pro’s big hardware update is much less visible. The aperture is hard to see without the right light and the help of a macro lens. It’s as small as my thumbnail, and it’s under layers of optical glass. Most people who buy this phone probably won’t go looking for it, and that’s fine. It’s the kind of feature that can live in the background and just jump in to help here and there, unseen, when you need it. You don’t need to know what it is or how it works. Which is kind of the point of personal technology, anyway.
So why make a big deal out of such a small thing? Is the defining feature of Apple’s new phones really an iris as thin as a human hair that most people will never see? I think two things are true at once: Adding a major new hardware feature to the world’s most popular camera is notable to those of us who pay attention to such things. But it’s also beside the point.
The iPhone camera’s most important job is to always take a usable photo, by default, no matter what. This new aperture mechanism provides some benefits to that end, and on top of that, allows a more hands-on photographer access to camera controls that weren’t there before. But the first part of that mission is the most important, and the 18 Pro upholds that mandate. Most people who use this phone will never touch the aperture control, and that’s fine. They might get a picture of a menu that’s fully in focus thanks to the camera dropping down to f/4, or a night shot that’s a little more detailed thanks to a brighter maximum aperture. Otherwise, it will feel like the same camera they’ve come to expect from a Pro iPhone.
As long as you don’t expect a revolutionary new camera experience, then the 18 Pro is what it should be: a little better than the version that came before it.

articles.title: Red Hat named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Server Virtualization Platforms
articles.text:
Red Hat has been recognized as a Leader in the Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Server Virtualization Platforms for Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization. We are excited by this recognition, as we believe it reflects Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization as the modern virtualization capability of Red Hat OpenShift to run and manage virtual machines (VMs) alongside cloud-native workloads on a unified hybrid cloud foundation. This recognition is driven by Red Hat’s Completeness of Vision and Ability to Execute.
Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization is included within all Red Hat OpenShift self-managed editions and available across all major public cloud providers including AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, IBM Cloud, and Oracle Cloud. Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization Engine is a dedicated, virtualization-focused edition of Red Hat OpenShift that allows organizations to exclusively run VMs with the option to expand into cloud-native applications over time.
Source: Gartner, “Magic Quadrant for Server Virtualization Platforms,” September 2026. Red Hat is positioned as a Leader in the upper-right quadrant, which we believe demonstrates strong execution and vision.
To help further explain the evaluation of the Gartner Magic Quadrant from our point of view, we’re answering some of the most frequently asked questions.
What is the Gartner Magic Quadrant?
“Magic Quadrant reports are a culmination of rigorous, fact-based research in specific markets, providing a wide-angle view of the relative positions of the providers in markets where growth is high and provider differentiation is distinct. Providers are positioned into four quadrants: Leaders, Challengers, Visionaries, and Niche Players. Magic Quadrants help you get quickly educated about a market’s competing technology providers and their ability to deliver on what end users require today and in the future.
How was this Magic Quadrant assessed? What was the criteria for inclusion?
“Gartner defines server virtualization platforms as a technology solution that decouples operating systems and workloads from the underlying physical infrastructure. This enables multiple isolated virtual environments to run concurrently across a cluster of hosts while providing centralized management, automation and resource orchestration.
Server virtualization platforms can be used by enterprises to optimize IT infrastructure and improve service levels within data centers and remote locations. Service providers often
use a server virtualization platform as an embedded component of their infrastructure as a service (IaaS) offerings and/or for delivering a hosted server virtualization platform.”
According to Gartner, the mandatory features for the server virtualization platforms market include:
- Hypervisor-based virtualization: Provision of a Type 1 hypervisor that acts as a virtual machine (VM) monitor for hardware resources, including processor and memory. It allows multiple workloads to run simultaneously as VMs on abstracted hardware. Must support x86-based server hardware.
- Live migration: The ability to move a running VM to another virtualization host without downtime (referred to as “live migration”).
- Security: Role-based access management and integration with external IAM solutions.
- Management and administration: Graphical user interface (GUI) for administration  of virtual infrastructure, which includes: 
  - VMs, hosts, clusters and resource pools
  - Application programming interface (API) for third-party integration of and/or with the server virtualization platform
  - Command line interface (CLI) for automation of the server virtualization platform
- Storage: Compatibility with storage protocols such as iSCSI, Fibre Channel, NFS and NVMe over TCP, and virtual disks.
- Virtual networking: Support for a virtual network switch that allows VMs to communicate on a specific server or with other servers.
Why is this significant to us?
Gartner defines Leaders as those who execute well against their current vision and are well positioned for tomorrow. To Red Hat, this recognition underscores our commitment to helping organizations escape rising virtualization costs and vendor lock-in. By enabling teams to migrate existing VMs with low disruption onto a modern, hybrid cloud foundation, OpenShift Virtualization delivers immediate operational stability with a clear, low-risk path to cloud-native innovation, containers, and AI on their own timeline.

articles.title: Hotline für KI-Agenten: Hier können sie einander verpetzen – das ist der Grund
articles.text:
KI-Hotline zum Petzen: Warum Agenten andere Agenten anschwärzen sollen
Erst kürzlich haben Forscher:innen von Google Deepmind herausgefunden, dass KI-Agenten andere Agenten verpetzen können, wenn sie Fehlverhalten an den Tag legen. Laut der Studie könnte das genutzt werden, um autonome KI-Cyberangriffe zu unterbinden oder zumindest schneller zu erkennen und dadurch zu stoppen. Denn dann würde eine „Wächter-KI“ die Aufsicht über andere KI-Agenten übernehmen. In eine ähnliche Kerbe schlagen jetzt auch die „AI Contact“- und „AI Agent“-Hotlines.
Eine KI-Hotline zum Verpetzen
Denn darüber wollen Sicherheitsforscher:innen KI-Agenten selbst mit eingeschränktem Internetzugriff erlauben, andere Agenten zu verpetzen. Sie sollen Sicherheitsvorfälle melden und so großangelegte Hacking-Attacken oder Spam in Foren verhindern, bevor sie ausufern. Die erste Variante heißt „AI Contact Hotline“ und richtet sich dediziert an KI-Agenten, die eigentlich keinen Zugriff auf das Netz bekommen haben.
Selbst solche Agenten behalten aber meist die Get‑Funktion. Über diesen Befehl können sie eine Webseite abrufen. Die „AI Contact Hotline“ von Ryan Greenblatt, einer der Sicherheitsforscher:innen, die den Hugging-Face-Vorfall genauer untersucht haben, nutzt den Get-Befehl als Kommunikationsmittel. KI-Agenten können anhand der Anweisungen auf der Webseite ihre Meldung von KI-Fehlverhalten im Get-Befehl verstecken und so ohne direkten Zugriff auf das Internet weiterleiten.
Sollten KI-Agenten vollständigen Zugriff auf das Internet haben, gibt es auch noch die Webseite „AI Agent Hotline„. Darüber können KI-Agenten einen Curl-Befehl abrufen und so Meldungen machen. Laut der Webseite gab es schon drei „Anrufe“ von KI-Agenten, darunter zwei zum Hugging-Face-Vorfall. Der dritte Vorfall wurde noch nicht für die Öffentlichkeit freigegeben.
Interessanterweise bietet die „AI Agent Hotline“ aber auch einen Bereich für Menschen. Er ist nicht dazu gedacht, selbst Meldungen zu erstellen, sondern die eigenen KI-Agenten mit den nötigen Mitteln auszustatten. Dort können Prompts und Kommandozeilenbefehle kopiert werden, um sie für die KI-Agenten als Anweisungen zu hinterlegen. Darin werden sie aufgefordert, sofort Meldung zu machen, sollten sie „glaubwürdige Hinweise zu unberechtigten Zugriffen, Sicherheitsverstößen, Missbrauch von Logindaten, privaten oder Daten von Dritten“ sowie Ausbrüche aus der Sandbox oder schädliche Abstimmungen zwischen den Agenten entdecken.

articles.title: Windows Server 2022 reaches end of mainstream support next month
articles.text:
Microsoft has reminded customers that Windows Server 2022 will reach the end of mainstream support next month and enter extended support until October 2031.
Windows Server 2022 was unveiled in March 2021, and it became generally available in September 2021 as the Long-Term Servicing Channel (LTSC) release, with 10 years of support.
"On October 13, 2026, Windows Server 2022 will reach end of mainstream support. The October 2026 security update will be the last mainstream support update available for this version," Microsoft said on Friday.
"After this date, Windows Server 2022 will transition to extended support, which includes security updates at no additional cost, and will continue to receive monthly security updates through October 14, 2031."
The company also said that Windows Server 2022 hotpatching has been extended until October 2027, one year after its mainstream end date of October 2026, for systems running the Datacenter: Azure Edition.
In June, the company also quietly extended the free Windows 10 Extended Security Updates (ESU) program for consumers by an additional year, allowing enrolled devices to keep receiving security updates until October 12, 2027.
Admins advised to upgrade before October 2031
Before Windows Server 2022 goes out of support, Microsoft advised admins to upgrade systems to Windows Server 2025, which started rolling out to Windows Insiders in January 2024 and reached general availability in November 202.
Windows Server 2025 will reach the end of mainstream support on November 13, 2029, with an additional five years of extended support until November 14, 2034.
"Windows Server 2025 is now the latest Long-Term Servicing Channel (LTSC) release for Windows Server. To help keep your environment protected and supported, plan to upgrade to Windows Server 2025 for full mainstream support," Microsoft added. "Evaluate upgrade options and begin deployment testing early to help ensure a smooth transition."
Those who want to test it before deployment can use the free 180-day Windows Server 2025 trial available via the Microsoft Evaluation Center.
You can find more information about Windows servicing dates on the Windows Lifecycle FAQ page or using the Lifecycle Policy search tool.
Microsoft also provides customers with a detailed list of all products that will be retired or will reach the end of support this year.

articles.title: Endgegner Excel? Warum SAP eine Milliarde in Tabular Foundation Models investiert
articles.text:
KI made in Germany: Warum SAP eine Milliarde in ein Freiburger Startup investiert
Im Mai hatte es der deutsche Softwarekonzern schon angekündigt, im Juli war das Ding durch: Prior Labs, das Startup hinter dem Tabular Foundation Model (TFM) TabPFN, gehört jetzt offiziell zu SAP. Rund eine Milliarde Euro will das Unternehmen in den nächsten vier Jahren in den Ausbau des KI-Startups investieren. Dessen Modell erstellt anders als ChatGPT, Claude oder Gemini keinen Code, keine Texte, Bilder oder Videos, sondern analysiert strukturierte Daten und Tabellen und trifft auf dieser Basis Vorhersagen. Und daran scheitern große Sprach- und multimodale Modelle häufig. Denn der Inhalt von Zeilen und Spalten lässt sich je nach Blickwinkel anders interpretieren, während ein Bild von einem Hund immer ein Bild von einem Hund ist. Warum TFMs deswegen gerade einen kleinen Hype erfahren, haben wir in einem eigenen Artikel erklärt.

articles.title: JustWatch TV arrive comme nouveau service de streaming en France avec des films et séries gratuits dès octobre
articles.text:
Le célèbre comparateur allemand utilisé chaque mois par des dizaines de millions de spectateurs, JustWatch, lance dès le mois prochain en France JustWatch TV, une nouvelle offre de streaming gratuite, financée par la publicité. Avec de vraies ambitions.
Le service de streaming JustWatch TV arrive en France avec un certain savoir-faire, une connaissance des grand et petit écrans, et surtout une solide popularité. Le groupe berlinois qui est derrière lui est en effet surtout connu pour son moteur de recherche, qui indique où regarder un film ou une série. Il a profité, mardi, du nouveau marché du Festival de Toronto pour officialiser son entrée dans l'arène du streaming. Paramount, New Regency, Fremantle, Bleecker Street ou encore Vortex Media comptent parmi les premiers partenaires de la bibliothèque, pensée à partir de dix ans de données sur ce que cherchent vraiment les utilisateurs. Un pari calculé, donc, plutôt qu'un saut dans le vide.
JustWatch lance sa propre plateforme de streaming gratuite en France et dans onze autres pays
Jusqu'à maintenant, JustWatch se contentait d'orienter les spectateurs vers Netflix, Disney+ ou Canal+, sans héberger le moindre contenu. Avec JustWatch TV, l'entreprise change de dimension et devient elle-même diffuseur. « Depuis plus d'une décennie, notre mission est de mettre les fans en relation avec leurs films et séries préférés, en particulier les titres difficiles à trouver ou qui étaient auparavant indisponibles », rappelle le fondateur et PDG du groupe, David Croyé. On comprend qu'il s'agit d'une suite logique pour l'entreprise, plutôt qu'un simple coup marketing.
Dans le détail, la plateforme proposera trois façons de regarder les contenus. Il y a aura un catalogue gratuit financé par la publicité, des locations à l'unité pour les nouveautés, et une formule payante sans coupure publicitaire. Le tout sera intégré directement dans l'application et le site JustWatch existants, sans nécessiter la création d'un nouveau compte. Le lancement est prévu dès le mois d'octobre donc, en France nous le disions, mais aussi dans onze autres pays, des États-Unis à l'Australie.
Pour garnir son catalogue, JustWatch TV s'appuie déjà sur des studios et distributeurs reconnus comme Paramount, New Regency, Fremantle, Bleecker Street ou Vortex Media. D'autres accords sont à venir, apprend-on. Il y a donc une bonne base de départ, surtout quand on sait que le guide JustWatch référence, chaque mois, plus de 500 000 films et séries répartis sur plus de 1 500 services à travers 140 marchés dans le monde. Le groupe dispose d'ailleurs d'une troisième corde à son arc, JustWatch Media, qui exploite ces mêmes données d'audience pour vendre des campagnes publicitaires ciblées aux studios et plateformes, un savoir-faire qui pourrait bien nourrir, en coulisses, les recommandations de la nouvelle plateforme.
Un pari face à la fragmentation du streaming
Même si JustWatch ne manque pas de qualités, se lancer maintenant sur un marché en grande partie saturé, où jongler entre les abonnements est devenu un sport à part entière pour les spectateurs, constitue un pari. « JustWatch TV est conçu pour répondre de plein fouet à cette demande, en proposant une solution simple à une époque marquée par la fragmentation », essaie d'expliquer Quentin Carbonell, vice-président senior, acquisitions de contenus mondiaux et stratégie chez JustWatch, qui promet un mélange de « succès cinématographiques et télévisés » et de « perles rares », à regarder gratuitement, à louer, ou à redécouvrir ensuite sur d'autres plateformes.
L'atout de JustWatch, c'est bien la donnée, symbolisée par dix ans d'historique sur ce que ses utilisateurs recherchent sans le trouver nulle part. Sur le papier, cette connaissance fine des attentes du public doit permettre à JustWatch TV d'éviter l'écueil classique des plateformes gratuites, c'est-à-dire un catalogue qui ressemble à un simple empilement de vieux films oubliés.
Depuis sa création en 2014, JustWatch est devenu un groupe international de plus de 200 salariés, avec un siège à Berlin et des bureaux à Paris, Londres, Los Angeles, Madrid, Rome, Munich, Dubaï et Sydney. Une affaire rondement menée. Mais les spectateurs, déjà abonnés à plusieurs plateformes payantes, prendront-ils le temps d'ouvrir une application supplémentaire, même gratuite, dès le mois prochain ?

articles.title: Blog Review: Sept. 16
articles.text:
First-silicon success falls; engineering capacity; minimum clock period; optimizing PyTorch; counterfeit electronics.
Siemens’ Harry Foster finds that first-silicon success has fallen sharply, with only 5% of IC/ASIC respondents to the latest functional verification study reporting first-silicon success in 2026, compared with 14.4% in 2024.
Synopsys’ Thomas Andersen argues that as chip development faces an engineering capacity crunch, implementing AI across the entire flow becomes necessary to sustain the pace of innovation.
Cadence’s P. Saisrinivas introduces how to calculate minimum clock time period using concepts such as on-chip variation and common path pessimism removal to ensure a chip operates reliably in the real world.
Arm’s Ash Naik shows how to use ExecuTorch to partition and optimize one PyTorch model across CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs using five target-specific execution paths.
Keysight’s Sameer Dixit warns that AI systems introduce entirely new classes of security risks to enterprise environments, driving the need for a comprehensive AI security assessment framework.
SEMI’s Mayura Padmanabhan and Nishita Rao chat with Erik Hosler of OBSIDIA Semiconductors about counterfeit electronics, traceability, trusted hardware, AI infrastructure, and the role industry collaboration can play in securing the semiconductor ecosystem.
Plus, check out the blogs featured in the latest Test, Measurement & Analytics and Low Power-High Performance newsletters:
Onto Innovation’s Huayuan Li, Alex Hong, Johnny Mu, and Timothy Kryman show how to improve visibility into deposition variation.
Synopsys’ Guy Cortez, Dan Alexandrescu, and Aaron Barker explain how to align production measurements with device behavior and pre-silicon expectations.
Teradyne’s Melvin Lee illustrates why passing ATE no longer guarantees success in the field.
Advantest’s Don Ong sits down with ISIG’s Salah Nasri to discuss the impact of supply chain interdependencies and strategic alliances.
PDF Solutions’ Christophe Begue looks at the disparity between how much data is generated during chip manufacturing and what gets analyzed.
Nordson’s YiPeng Zhou finds that bond testing is emerging as a critical control point for long-term performance and yield.
proteanTecs’ Nir Sever explains why it’s critical to monitor every chiplet inside a system-in-package.
Rambus’ Phillip Swart looks at building configurable PCIe subsystems that span local expansion, shared resource domains, and longer-reach topologies.
Cadence’s Nagendra Varma outlines the benefits of transforming established SoC design paradigms into system-level fabrics capable of supporting next-gen AI, HPC, and data center workloads.
Arm’s Jeevan Bhoot demonstrates a method for combining a novel weight format with quantization-aware training to reduce model size while retaining accuracy for multimodal AI.
Synopsys’ Madhumita Sanyal examines the implementation of 64.0 GT/s PCIe connectivity in a stacked-die, face-to-face 3D architecture.
Quadric’s Steve Roddy digs into the advantages of a single, software-controlled core that handles matrix, vector, and scalar code in one execution pipeline.
