articles.title: How Hidden Triggers Can Make Robots Ignore Their Own Safety Rules
articles.text:
This article is brought to you by VicOne.
Robot safety has traditionally asked: Can a machine remain safe when something goes wrong? Physical AI raises a harder question: Can a machine remain safe when an attacker changes what it sees, decides, or does even when nothing appears to have failed?
As AI and robotics continue to advance at an unprecedented pace, modern robots perceive through multimodal sensors, interpret context using AI models, and translate those interpretations into physical action. As they move into dynamic environments, their safety increasingly depends on the integrity of the data guiding their decisions.
That dependence creates risks that conventional safety assessments may not fully capture. Recent research has demonstrated that manipulating what a robot sees, hears, or interprets can influence its behavior without requiring direct control.
Such manipulation can occur anywhere across its complex sensing and decision-making system — a layered attack surface encompassing training pipelines, system infrastructure, and runtime perception.
Layer One: Corrupting intelligence at its source
In 2017, BadNets demonstrated that a model could behave normally under most conditions, yet fail in the presence of a specific hidden trigger. In one example, a subtle pattern caused a stop sign to be misclassified as a speed limit sign without affecting the model’s behavior on other inputs.
What began as a classification vulnerability has since evolved into action manipulation.
At NeurIPS 2025, researchers introduced BadVLA a backdoor attack targeting Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models that allow robots to see, interpret instructions, and produce coordinated physical movement. Rather than altering a single label, the attack caused conditional deviations in the robot’s action trajectory when a trigger was present. Without the trigger, the model largely preserved normal task performance, while the backdoor remained effective under task transfers and model fine-tuning.
A related study in 2025, GoBA, showed that ordinary objects such as a coffee mug could serve as a reliable trigger. The researchers reported a 97 percent attack success rate without degrading performance on clean inputs.
A critical safety question today is whether Physical AI models remain within their task and safety boundaries under adversarial conditions.
These studies expose a blind spot in model validation: A model may pass testing yet produce corrupted behavior when a hidden trigger appears in operation.
So a critical safety question today is whether Physical AI models remain within their task and safety boundaries under adversarial conditions. Simulation tools such as NVIDIA Isaac Sim, when paired with VicOne Radeis, can test the effects of manipulated inputs before deployment.
VicOne LAB R7 demonstrates Radeis, a Physical AI safety validator for NVIDIA Isaac Sim that tests how adversarial visual inputs affect robot behavior before deployment.VicOne
Layer Two: System vulnerabilities as gateways to AI control
Even a securely trained model can be subverted if the surrounding system stack is vulnerable.
In September 2025, researchers disclosed UniPwn, a Bluetooth exploit chain affecting quadruped and humanoid robots from a major manufacturer. Hardcoded cryptographic keys allowed traffic decryption, authentication checks were bypassed, and command injection enabled root-level execution. The exploit is also described as “wormable.” A compromised robot could scan nearby units and potentially affect an entire fleet.
VicOne Lab R7’s demo shows how chaining three wireless exploits can trigger uncontrolled robot behavior within 60 seconds, resulting in operational disruption.VicOne
Middleware creates another exposure point. Vulnerabilities in ROS 2 and DDS-based systems can enable arbitrary code execution or abuse unauthenticated topics to deliver malicious commands. With sufficient access, an attacker could override motor commands or replace AI model weights without directly attacking the model architecture.
In this case, the components may still function as designed. What has changed is the trustworthiness of the commands flowing through the system. Vulnerability management can help teams identify known risks before deployment, while continuous monitoring can surface emerging threats.
Layer Three: Manipulating perception and reasoning at runtime
At runtime, manipulating inputs that shape perception or reasoning may require neither firmware modification nor a network breach.
In 2024, RoboPAIR demonstrated how carefully structured prompts could redirect LLM-controlled robots into unsafe trajectories. BadRobot exposed a deeper architectural weakness: in several cases, a robot verbally refused a dangerous command while its motion controller executed the action anyway.
Vision-based manipulation is equally powerful. VLAttack showed that an adversarial patch within the camera’s view could reduce a VLA model’s task success rate to zero. FreezeVLA showed that a single adversarial image could freeze a robot’s decision-making loop, making it unresponsive to subsequent instructions.
Runtime assurance must therefore look beyond whether individual components remain available and assess whether cyber events are beginning to affect physical behavior.
In each case, the camera may still work, the model may still run, and the controller may still respond. Yet the resulting behavior can be unsafe because the robot is acting on manipulated perception or reasoning.
Runtime assurance must therefore look beyond whether individual components remain available and assess whether cyber events are beginning to affect physical behavior. Security event correlation, behavioral-impact assessment, and policy-bounded response supported by edge AI, can help contain the affected path without unnecessarily stopping the entire robot fleet.
From point-in-time safety to lifecycle assurance
The risks across these three layers reveal the missing layer in robot safety assurance: cybersecurity. Functional safety addresses failures and unexpected operating conditions; cybersecurity extends that assurance to deliberate manipulation, including attacks that may leave the underlying system apparently functional.
This requires assurance across the robot’s lifecycle. During design, teams need to understand which cyber risks could invalidate assumptions behind intended behavior. Before deployment, they should test whether realistic attacks can cause a robot to deviate from its task or safety boundaries. In operation, monitoring should identify whether cyber events are beginning to affect behavior, contain the affected path, and preserve safe operation where possible.
VicOne’s lifecycle approach combines AI model and vulnerability scanning, simulation-based validation, and continuous monitoring to help secure robots from development through operation.VicOne
While cybersecurity does not replace functional safety, it helps ensure that Physical AI remains within acceptable boundaries even when what it sees, decides, or does is under attack.
For a deeper look at the cybersecurity risks and defense strategies shaping autonomous robotics, download our whitepaper “Securing the Rise of AI Robots: Cyber Risks, Real-World Threats, and Defense Strategies.”
VicOne is a Physical AI cybersecurity company protecting vehicles and robots from cyber threats that can alter behavior and compromise safety. Headquartered in Tokyo, Japan, the company provides automotive and robotics organizations with software and services to identify cyber risks early, assess their potential safety impact, and protect systems in operation, helping maintain safe, reliable behavior across real-world deployments.

articles.title: Ist Diversität jetzt weniger relevant?
articles.text:
Diversität im Backlash: Was Unternehmen jetzt tun sollten
Die öffentliche Aufmerksamkeit für Diversität in Unternehmen schwindet: In den USA werden DEI-Programme reihenweise eingestellt, auch in Deutschland rückt das Thema in den Hintergrund. Isabelle Gardt, CMO von OMR und Initiatorin der Initiative OMR 5050, beschäftigt sich seit 2018 mit Gleichstellung in der Arbeitswelt. Den Wandel beobachtet sie auch mit Frust. Gleichzeitig sieht sie in der Vergangenheit Fehler, die es zu korrigieren gilt.
Im Interview bei t3n Arbeit in Progress gibt sie Einblicke in konkrete Maßnahmen, spricht über Frustration und erklärt, was dem Thema geschadet hat. Das Interview ist gekürzt, das vollständige Gespräch gibt es in der verlinkten Podcast-Folge.
t3n: Diversitätsinitiativen werden abgebaut, das Thema verliert an Aufmerksamkeit. Waren die Erwartungen an Diversität in Unternehmen zu groß?
Isabelle Gardt: Ich glaube nicht, dass sie zu groß waren. Die Herausforderung war, dass bei Diversität – das ist ja auch einfach ein sehr großes Buzzword – nicht sofort Ergebnisse sichtbar werden und es sehr schwer ist, damit einen Return on Invest zu verbinden. Viele Menschen hatten Erwartungen, die nicht erfüllt wurden. Und mit den fehlenden Ergebnissen wandert das Thema jetzt einfach wieder aufs Abstellgleis.
Hat das Thema Diversität in der öffentlichen Wahrnehmung seinen Zenit erreicht?
Bei der öffentlichen Aufmerksamkeit würde ich fast ja sagen, leider. Um die Pandemie herum war es sehr aufmerksamkeitsstark. Fast jedes Unternehmen wollte sich dazu positionieren. Aber wenn wir auf die Zielerreichung schauen, dann haben wir den Höhepunkt leider auf gar keinen Fall erreicht. Wenn wir jetzt auf die DAX-Vorstände schauen, dann ist der Frauenanteil nochmal gesunken. Dazu erleben wir gerade einen Backlash, die Entwicklung läuft rückschrittlich. Deswegen ist die nachlassende Aufmerksamkeit eher problematisch. Da müssen wir jetzt schauen, wie wir wieder Fortschritt ermöglichen, ohne erhobenen Zeigefinger – denn darauf haben die meisten Menschen einfach keine Lust.
Was wäre denn so ein typisch erhobener Zeigefinger?
Oft bekomme ich mit, wie auf Aussagen mit „Nein, so kannst du das nicht sagen“ reagiert wird. Das fördert die Reaktion mit „Jetzt darf ich aber gar nichts mehr sagen“. Am besten funktioniert es, rund um das ganze Thema Diversität möglichst sachlich zu erklären, ohne Ermahnungen. Ich merke übrigens, wie das Thema in Unternehmen zwar nicht mehr so öffentlichkeitsstark ist, aber dennoch weiter daran gearbeitet wird. Wahrscheinlich ist das der Weg, den wir jetzt gehen müssen, auch, wenn ich das schade finde. Ich kenne auch HR‑ler, die sich dazu austauschen und Step-by-Step das Thema weiter vorantreiben wollen. Und auch wenn Initiativen eingestellt werden: Diversity ist ja nicht auf einmal weg. Die Bemühungen, die sie vorher hatten, sind noch da. Diverse Teams werden sie weiter vorantreiben.
Was steckt denn hinter eurer Arbeit mit OMR 50/50?
Wir haben 2018 angefangen, das Thema Gleichstellung zu bearbeiten, weil wir gesehen haben, dass die Bühnen bei OMR absolut nicht 50-50 waren. Da waren einfach sehr viel mehr Männer auf den Bühnen als Frauen. Ich selbst habe dazu einen Tech-Background und war ganz oft die einzige Frau im Raum. 2018 haben wir einen Masterclass-Raum für 200 Personen versucht zu füllen, und wurden total überrannt. Daraus sind schließlich eine eigene OMR‑Bühne, ein Podcast, Community-Events, ein Newsletter und eine Social-Plattform. Ab 2022 hatten wir eine eigenen Stage bis 2024, jetzt integrieren wir das Thema in das große OMR‑Rahmenprogramm. So wollen wir Leute mitnehmen, die sich nicht auf den Weg zu der eigenen Bühne machen würden.
Dennoch hat das Thema keine eigene Bühne mehr. Ist es denn auch weniger wichtig? Oder ist das ein Beispiel für eine Weiterentwicklung einer Maßnahme?
Das zuerst genannte Feedback zur eigenen Bühne haben wir auch bekommen. Aber ich sehe das eigentlich nicht so. Die 50-50-Stage hatte eine Kapazität von 1000 bis 1200 Personen, die großen Bühnen liegen bei 5000 bis 7000. Aus meiner Sicht erreichen wir so mehr Menschen. Und das Ziel mit der Initiative ist, dass wir sie irgendwann nicht mehr brauchen, weil das Thema einfach so selbstverständlich und Teil des Alltags ist, dass wir irgendwann nicht mehr darüber sprechen müssen.
Was habt ihr in den vergangenen Jahren über Diversity-Arbeit gelernt?
Die meisten Fortschritte haben wir bei uns mit Unconscious-Bias-Workshops gesehen. Da wirst du dir selbst über deine versteckten Vorurteile bewusst. Wie bewerte ich etwa Bewerber:innen? Dazu haben wir Allyship-Trainings gemacht, in denen es darum geht, für jemanden einzustehen, der unterdrückt wird. Das fängt schon an, wenn jemand immer wieder im Meeting unterbrochen wird. Das auch gerade Männern näherzubringen, die sich ihrer Privilegien oft gar nicht bewusst sind, hat bei uns sehr viel geholfen. Dazu haben wir Stellenausschreibungen angepasst, sie in anderen Communitys gepostet. Und wir lassen das Team im Newsletter von persönlichen Erfahrungen berichten. Es sind oft Kleinigkeiten, die aber einen Unterschied machen.
Ob Qouten aus Sicht von Gardt sinnvoll sind, was bei Diversitätsbemühungen falsch gelaufen ist und mit welcher Entwicklung sie bei dem Thema rechnet, hört ihr in der verlinkten Folge von t3n Arbeit in Progress.
Podcast t3n Arbeit in Progress anhören
Ihr könnt den Podcast t3n Arbeit in Progress bequem in der Podcast-App eurer Wahl abonnieren. In der Regel findet ihr den Podcast einfach über die Eingabe „t3n Arbeit in Progress“ in der Suche. Ansonsten könnt ihr auch den RSS-Feed manuell in der App eingeben.

articles.title: Playing both sides of the U.S.-China AI “Cold War”
articles.text:
Saudi Arabia celebrated the launch of what it calls the world’s most advanced Arabic-language AI model earlier this month. The technology behind it came from China even as the kingdom spends billions building its AI infrastructure with American companies.
The Arabic model, Humain-m3, is based on an open-source system from Chinese startup MiniMax. Humain, the state-backed company that commissioned the model, has struck major deals with Nvidia and other U.S. technology companies to build its AI computing capacity.
Saudi Arabia is not alone. From Latin America to Southeast and Central Asia, countries are buying American chips while adopting Chinese open-source models, splitting key AI projects between companies from two AI superpowers. The trend presents a growing complication for Washington’s competition with Beijing. Even countries investing heavily in American AI infrastructure are not necessarily choosing American technology for every layer of the AI stack.
“Many countries around the world, particularly in the Global South, want the best of both worlds,” Kyle Chan, a fellow at the John L. Thornton China Center at the Brookings Institution, told Rest of World. Many countries often do not attach the same security stigma to Chinese technology that Washington does, Chan said. “Ultimately, many countries around the world want to keep their options open and not be too dependent on any single source of technology.”
Staying in the middle
In August, Brazil announced an investment worth roughly $444 million into AI, which it effectively divided between Chinese and American technologies.
Around $255 million will go toward supercomputing infrastructure in Rio de Janeiro, developed in partnership with China’s HuaweiHuaweiHuawei is a Chinese technology company focused on mobile phones and telecommunications, and is seen as a poster child for China’s global tech ambitions.READ MORE and iFlytek. The rest, around $189 million, will go to a separate supercomputer that Brazil is currently tendering, but expecting to source from Nvidia.
“The strategy is not to depend on a single company, technology or country,” President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s administration said in a statement, adding that the investments were intended to strengthen Brazil’s sovereignty over its data.
For most countries, technological sovereignty does not mean building an entire AI stack at home, Jesse Marks, a China-Middle East research scholar at the Australian National University, told Rest of World. Competing at the frontier has become prohibitively expensive, leaving governments to decide which technologies they can develop themselves and where they must rely on foreign suppliers.
For Saudi Arabia, it would be a “natural decision” to choose Chinese foundations for sovereign AI models if they perform better on relevant benchmarks, even if doing so carries political consequences with Washington, Marks said.
The U.S., however, has greater leverage in parts of the stack where its technology is harder to replace, such as advanced semiconductors, networking equipment, and sensitive cloud infrastructure. But Washington will struggle with countries that want AI but cannot afford American systems or software, Marks said.
“Outside of the network of American partners who are trusted or can afford it, it’s Chinese AI. It’s open models,” he said.
These technological choices are also becoming intertwined with countries’ broader diplomatic relationships. “AI is one of a number of portfolios that middle powers have to consider when negotiating with a partner like the United States,” Marks said.
Washington has accused Chinese labs of “free-riding” and training their models from frontier American AI models at an “industrial scale.” China, having rejected those accusations, has warned it would retaliate if Washington implements any curbs on Chinese AI companies.
China catching up
Chinese companies are ramping up efforts to compete with American companies on different layers of the AI stack.
In Egypt, Huawei has bid to build AI data centers for the government, according to a source-based report by Bloomberg, competing against a proposal involving Nvidia. A successful bid would give Chinese companies another foothold in a market where AI infrastructure has so far been dominated by American technology.
Southeast Asia is another region where China-U.S. competition over technological influence is increasingly apparent.
Washington launched the U.S.-ASEAN AI Spark initiative in July, offering financial and technical support to Southeast Asian governments interested in adopting American AI technologies for public-sector use.
Malaysia is considering going in another direction, evaluating Huawei’s Ascend 910C accelerators as the backbone of its sovereign AI initiative, Bloomberg reported.
The U.S. or China?
For now, the two AI superpowers appear to be taking different approaches to building influence abroad.
“China, like any leading power, wants the world to function in a manner that furthers its interests and replicates its own values,” Arindrajit Basu, a doctoral researcher in global governance of emerging technology at Leiden University, told Rest of World. “In the case of the internet and its allied technologies, this is a vision of governance providing a greater preference to the state in maintaining public order and security online. However, China is yet to engage in the naked coercion we have seen from the Trump administration that has reportedly clearly laid out an ultimatum.”
Washington is considering warning against countries trying to align with both U.S.- and China-led AI initiatives. That could put countries already engaging with both sides in a difficult position.
Kazakhstan, for example, has joined the U.S.-led Pax Silica initiative, which aims to build secure AI supply chains spanning semiconductors, compute, and other critical technologies. It has also joined China’s World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, or WAICO, which focuses on cooperation on AI development and governance. Uzbekistan signaled its intention to engage with both organizations last month.
Basu said the two initiatives currently have different aims.
Pax Silica is an invitation-only grouping focused on sharing critical resources among its members. WAICO, by contrast, is open to countries globally and presents itself as a governance body complementary to the United Nations. It is not currently tied directly to sharing computing resources or research.
“So, ideally China would want countries to choose, but I think it realizes that an ultimatum is unrealistic at this stage. Hence, we will see the more norms-oriented diplomacy that slowly but surely gets countries to use Chinese products and engage with Chinese capacity-building efforts,” Basu said.
Chan warned that Washington’s approach could instead encourage countries to preserve ties with both sides.
“Washington’s efforts to force other countries to pick a side will face growing pushback. Even close allies, such as Europe, are rethinking their dependency on American technology. Third countries will want to maintain flexibility and independence by working with both the U.S. and China,” he said.
Singapore could be an early test. A founding signatory of Pax Silica, the country has publicly acknowledged receiving an invitation to join the China-led AI organization and said it is considering the offer.
“We engage different countries through a range of multilateral and bilateral platforms,” Singapore’s Minister for Digital Development and Information, Josephine Teo, told Parliament last week. “The engagements arise at different times, serve different purposes, and evolve as our interests and circumstances change.”

articles.title: Mozilla and Mistral partner to expand AI competition, user choice | The Mozilla Blog
articles.text:
Mozilla and Mistral: Partnering to expand AI competition and preserve user choice
The AI race is shifting. Again. Practically overnight, competition has expanded from “which AI model is best?” to a new high-stakes battle over which models people can access, through which products, and whether people have meaningful choice about AI at all.
In response, Mozilla and Mistral today announced a partnership built on a shared idea: a new, open-source AI model alternative to Big Tech-default browser ecosystems. The intent: a model deliberately designed to keep the web open to technological diversity, competition, and choice.
And we’re putting this idea into practice in Firefox.
Mistral Small 4 is coming to Firefox Smart Window beta (learn more about Firefox Smart Window here), becoming a new AI model for Smart Window users in the US and Canada, while expanding Smart Window beta access and French-language support to Firefox users in France. Across all markets where Smart Window beta is available, Firefox users can still choose from a multitude of other AI models.
“AI is becoming part of how people experience the web every day. We want to make sure that doesn’t mean people are chained to one company’s self-serving pipeline. With the browser sitting at the heart of the web and online experience, it should be a place where different AI providers can compete and open source has a seat at the table.
This isn’t just a product partnership. A browser shouldn’t be a one-way funnel. It should preserve what made the internet powerful to begin with: the freedom to explore, discover different ideas and tech, and decide for ourselves where to go next,” said Anthony Enzor-DeMeo, CEO of Mozilla Corporation.
Choice and competition are worth protecting
As AI integration becomes increasingly concentrated, we are in jeopardy of a handful of closed-model companies controlling the browser, the search engine, the AI model, and the surrounding services that connect them. Mozilla and Mistral are betting that independent and interoperable models can offer an alternative to global tech monopolies controlling the next digital era.
“This partnership represents two open source advocates working together to bring Mistral’s scientific innovations to Mozilla’s consumers around the world. Together, we are bringing privacy, control, and choice to AI-powered web browsing,” said Arthur Mensch, Co-founder and CEO of Mistral.
Meaningful choice isn’t confined to personal preference for one AI model over another. Web products need to be able to work with different AI providers, and people deserve the option of switching without being locked into a single company’s ecosystem. When a tech layer as far-reaching and influential as AI is controlled by a small handful of players, it risks creating closed systems and closed doors, making it harder for new ideas and better technologies to grow, reach users, and compete on merits.
Mozilla and Mistral aim to keep that door open. The combination of an independent browser with a frontier European AI company gives people and institutions greater access to useful, responsible AI, the opposite of locking them into one company’s singular technology ecosystem.
Selecting Mistral, and expanding to France
Mozilla selected Mistral Small 4 after evaluating its performance for Smart Window Beta, including multilingual performance, an important part of the fit. The companies approached multilingual and multicultural tuning as a core model feature, rather than simply adapting an English-first experience for a new market.
For Firefox users, Mistral access starts with Smart Window Beta, a browsing experience designed to turn AI into a useful assistant for the things we do online: making sense of complex search trails, finding something valuable you clicked away from, presenting data sources, and generally picking up where day-to-day internet use got left off.
France is the first new market for Smart Window with official French-language support. Mozilla is planning additional European expansion later this year.
A different kind of AI competition
Our Mistral partnership puts an ambitious new AI model approach into practice: a multilingual, globally competitive European AI company reaching people through an independent browser, leveraging openness to create more room for new technologies to compete and succeed. Mistral can reach Firefox users without owning the browser, and Mozilla can integrate and recommend Mistral without removing user choice.
It is a natural extension of the principles that have shaped Firefox and the open web, and the kind of AI ecosystem we intend to continue building.
